translation_en:
Qiu Xiang, registered in Xiaogan County, De’an Prefecture, Huguang, belonged to a military household and was a student of the National University; he specialized in the Book of Odes, had the courtesy name Tingzuo, was second in birth order, and was aged forty, born on the twentieth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Fuyi; his grandfather, Wenbin; his father, Yuan, a county Registrar; his mother was née Lin, and his stepmothers were née Min and née Xie; both parents were living, his elder brother was Song, his younger brothers were Mo and Ji, and his wife was née Yan; he ranked forty-eighth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and seventy-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Jia Zongxi, registered in Changshu County, Suzhou Prefecture, Zhili, belonged to an artisan household and was a student of the National University; he specialized in the Book of Odes, had the courtesy name Yuanshan, was first in birth order, and was aged thirty-six, born on the twenty-first day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shousi; his grandfather, Mengde; his father, Tingyu; and his mother, née Jia; his mother alone survived, his younger brothers were Zongsi and Zongli, and his wife was née Deng; he ranked fifty-eighth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and fortieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lin Shiyuan, registered in Sihui County, Zhaoqing Prefecture, Guangdong, belonged to a civilian household and was a county school student; he specialized in the Book of Odes, had the courtesy name Sishao, was first in birth order, and was aged twenty-three, born on the twenty-fourth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Huan, posthumously appointed a guard Registrar; his grandfather was Tai, a county Assistant Magistrate; his father was Xiang, and his mother was née Ouyang; his parents and at least one grandparent were living, his younger brothers were Shize, Shimei, Shi’an, and Shizhe, and his wife was née Ouyang; he ranked second in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 256th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Ge, registered in Dongyang County, Jinhua Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was a county school student; he specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals, had the courtesy name Zhengfu, was second in birth order, and was aged thirty-two, born on the seventh day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yuanding, posthumously appointed Assistant Censor-in-Chief; his grandfather was Gui; his father, Rong; and his mother, née Xu; both parents were living, his elder brother was Kai, a tribute scholar (gongshi), his younger brother was Bin, and his wife was née Wu; he ranked sixty-second in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 200th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
He Wenying, registered in a civilian household in Shunde County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Bangyan, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was forty-seven years old, born on the nineteenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhongxian, his grandfather Yuguang, his father Liang, and his mother née Huang; his mother alone was still living, his younger brothers were Wenzheng, Wencan, Wentai, and Wencong, and his wife was née Zhou; he placed nineteenth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and two hundred fifteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Daoli, registered in a civilian household in Qi County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, was an added-quota student of the county Confucian school specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Chengji, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was twenty-seven years old, born on the twentieth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shi, his grandfather Wen, his father Zhao, a county Vice Magistrate, and his mother née Wang; both parents were living, he married a woman née Xue and was subsequently betrothed to a woman née Nie; he placed fifty-fifth in the Henan Provincial Examination and three hundredth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Huang Xiang, registered in a military household in Luoshan County, Xinyang Subprefecture, Runing Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals; his courtesy name was Yanhe, he ranked second among his brothers, and he was forty-seven years old, born on the twentieth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Youliang, his grandfather Demao, his father Xin, a county Registrar, and his mother née Chen; his mother alone was still living, his elder brother was Zhen, his younger brother Xi, and his wife was née Chen; he placed forty-eighth in the Henan Provincial Examination and one hundred twenty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Du Yuan, registered in a civilian household in Changli County, Yongping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region (Zhili), was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Yongqing, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was thirty-two years old, born on the thirtieth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Fuli, his grandfather Min, granted the title of Secretary in the Ministry of Works, his father Qian, Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture, and his mother née Yang, granted the title of Lady of Peace; both parents were living, his younger brothers were Jun and Han, and his wife was née Tang; he placed seventy-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and fifty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Chu Cai 儲材, registered in Yixing County, Changzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education; he specialized in the Classic of Poetry, had the courtesy name Shizi, ranked third among his brothers, and was aged forty-three, born on the eighteenth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zuxue, a county-school instructor; his grandfather was Zonggan; and his father was Zhi, a tribute student; his father's former wife was née Li, and his mother was née Ge. Both parents were deceased; his elder brothers were Congshi [?] and Yongxi, and his wife was née Zhuge; he placed sixteenth in the Yingtian Provincial Examination and 131st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liao Chun 廖純, registered in Xinyu County, Linjiang Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education; he specialized in the Classic of Poetry, had the courtesy name Qianshun, ranked fifth among his brothers, and was aged forty, born on the seventh day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shizhong, his grandfather was Zhengyin, his father was Tongdao, and his mother was née He. His father was deceased and his mother living; his elder brothers were Long, Jian, Duan, and Gang, his younger brothers were Rou and Zhi, and his wife was née Huang; he placed twenty-sixth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and twenty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Chun 楊春, registered in Xindu County, Chengdu Prefecture, Sichuan, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education; he specialized in the Classic of Changes, had the courtesy name Yuanzhi, ranked third among his brothers, and was aged forty-six, born on the eleventh day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shixian, his grandfather was Shoushan, and his father was Wen, a subprefectural clerk; his father's former wives were née Guo and née Yang, and his mother was née Xiong. His father was deceased and his mother living; his elder brothers were Yuan and Zheng, his younger brothers were Hui and Zhe, and his wife was née Ye; he placed thirty-first in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and seventeenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cheng Yu 程愈, registered in Chun'an County, Yanzhou Prefecture [?], Zhejiang, belonged to a medical household and was a student of the Directorate of Education; he specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals, had the courtesy name Jiezhi, ranked first among his brothers, and was aged forty-four, born on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yizhong; his grandfather was Maozheng, a medical instructor; his father was Mingong, who held the prestige title Gentleman for Rendering Service; and his mother was née Fang. Both parents were deceased; he married a woman née Hu and subsequently a woman née Yu; he placed third in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 183rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

His great-grandfather was Chaozuo, his grandfather Zhongda, his father Rang, and his mother née Xu; his father was deceased and his mother living, his elder brother was Ren, and he married a woman née Deng. He placed thirty-ninth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 236th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tian Ji, registered in Luochuan County, Fu Subprefecture, Yan’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Wenyuan, he ranked third among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-eight, born on the seventeenth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Ximeng, his grandfather Zheng, and his father Yuan, a Registrar; his legal mother was née Yang, his stepmother née Li, and his birth mother née Zuo. His parents were deceased; his elder brothers were Zi and Run, and he married a woman née Guo. He placed twelfth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 199th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Zongsi, registered in Peng County, Chengdu Prefecture, Sichuan, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Xiyan, he ranked third among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-three, born on the fourteenth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Xiaoxiang, his grandfather Hai, and his father Qing, an Assistant Instructor; his father’s former wives were née Dong and née Zhang, and his mother was née Zhang. His parents were deceased; his elder brothers were Zonglian, an Assistant Instructor, and Zongxi, and he married a woman née Yang. He placed fifty-seventh in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and thirty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Shi, registered in Chengdu Central Guard under the Sichuan Regional Military Commission, belonged to a military official household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Weizhong, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was aged forty-one, born on the seventeenth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Fu, his grandfather Zhiguang, his father Qian, a Vice Battalion Commander, and his mother née Ni; both parents were living, his younger brothers were Xiao, Yang, Wan, and Kui, and he married a woman née Wang. translation_en:
Zheng Shi 鄭軾, courtesy name Shizhi, was registered in Yongfeng County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi, in a civilian household. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Documents, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-three, and born on the third day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Dade, his grandfather Yinglin, and his father Huai, a prefectural judge; his mother was née Yu. His mother alone was still living. His younger brothers were Zhi and Zhe, and his wife was née Hu. He ranked forty-ninth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 185th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Deng Huai 鄧淮, courtesy name Anji, was registered in Jishui County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi, in a civilian household. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Documents, he was sixth in birth order, aged forty-four, and born on the nineteenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wenyu, his grandfather Chonghe, and his father Jiazhen; his mother was née Pang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Anshi, an instructor in a medical school, Anshu, Anyuan, Anren, and Anxu; his wife was née Xiao. He ranked twelfth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and thirty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Shengzhi 劉盛之, courtesy name Wenyu, was registered in Dai Subprefecture, Taiyuan Prefecture, Shanxi, in a military household. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged twenty-eight, and born on the first day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Cai, his grandfather Hui, and his father Chang, vice magistrate of Daxing County; his mother was née Gao. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yizhi, Yingzhi, Wenzhi, Yuzhi [?], and Minzhi [?]; his wife was née Zhang. He ranked forty-sixth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and fifty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Qin 徐欽, courtesy name Jingzhi, was registered in a military household of the Embroidered-uniform Guard and was a native of Jiangning County, Yingtian Prefecture. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged forty-six, and born on the fourteenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Tian, his grandfather Fuguang, and his father Zhi; his mother was née Zhou. Both parents were deceased. His wife was née Kang. He ranked second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and ninety-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Liang Wen, courtesy name Guangfu, was registered in a civilian household in Longquan County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he was third in birth order, aged thirty-eight, and born on the fifth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather’s name is illegible (□); his grandfather was Kui, his father Yongchen, and his mother née Liu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Guangrong and Guanghua, and his wife was née Feng. He ranked thirty-seventh in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 134th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Gu Jingxiang, courtesy name Ruiqing, was registered in an artisan household in Daxing County, Shuntian Prefecture, and was a native of Changzhou County in the directly administered metropolitan region. A Confucian scholar specializing in the Book of Documents, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-nine, and born on the twentieth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wanyilang, his grandfather Wenxing, his father Zicheng, and his mother née He. His father was deceased, and he attended upon his surviving mother. He married a woman née Yang and subsequently became betrothed to a woman née Liang. He ranked 129th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventy-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liang Jing, courtesy name Deyu, was registered in a civilian household in Gaoyao County, Zhaoqing Prefecture, Guangdong. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he was second in birth order, aged forty-four, and born on the eighth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Boying, a County Registrar; his grandfather was Fuyin; his father was Shao, an Assistant Instructor; and his mother was née Feng. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Jiao, his younger brother Xiao, and his wife née Li. He ranked second in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 148th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Yuegao, courtesy name Yuanbai, was registered in a military household in Huangyan County, Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he was fifth in birth order, aged forty-six, and born on the twenty-third day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yili, his grandfather Fengxian, his father Tangzhi, and his mother née Teng. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Yuewei, Yuexiang, Yueding, and Yuesheng; his younger brothers were Yuehao, Yuemian, Yueyu, Yuechang, Yuejing, Yuechao, and Yuejing. His wife was née Xia. He ranked twelfth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and twenty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Chen Run, registered in an artisan household in Lin’an County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Weize, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-eight, born on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xing, his grandfather Wen, and his father Gui; his mother was née Zhao and his stepmother née Shen. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Jun and Cheng. He married a woman née Zhao and subsequently a woman née Shao. He placed fourteenth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 237th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Kai, registered in a civilian household in Rui’an County, Wenzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Classic of Changes; his courtesy name was Yunzhao, he ranked second among his brothers, and he was aged forty-four, born on the eighteenth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather Liang was posthumously granted the title of Left Administration Vice Commissioner; his grandfather Jingheng held that office. His father was Tan and his mother née Zhou. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Qi. He married a woman née He and subsequently a woman née Hu. He placed fifty-ninth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 156th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yu Xuan, registered in a civilian household in Lanxi County, Jinhua Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Classic of Changes; his courtesy name was Gongsu, he ranked third among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-eight, born on the eighth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Guanyi, his grandfather Mengxin, and his father Cunmei; his father’s former wife was née Shao and his mother née Gu. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Wei and Yu, and his younger brothers Zi and Nan. He married a woman née Fang. He placed fifty-fifth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 149th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yu Fengjie, registered in a civilian household in Laiyang County, Dengzhou Prefecture, Shandong, was a county government school student specializing in the Classic of Documents; his courtesy name was Shihe, he ranked second among his brothers, and he was aged twenty-seven, born on the seventeenth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Liquan; his grandfather Jingchang was posthumously granted the title of Director; his father Mao was Right Administration Assistant Commissioner; and his mother, née Zhang, was granted the title of Lady of Peace. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Fengming and his younger brother Fengyong. He was betrothed to a woman née Xu. He placed nineteenth in the Shandong [Provincial?] Examination (one character illegible) and eleventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhang Min, registered in Qimen County, Huizhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals; his courtesy name was Zhixue. First in birth order, he was aged thirty-three and was born on the twentieth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Sizhong, his grandfather Xiyong, and his father Wenhan; his mother was née Wu. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Kan, Jun, Fei, and Guang. He married a woman née Huang and subsequently a woman née Zhou. He placed sixty-second in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and twenty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xie Ji, registered in Le'an County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to an official household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Weixi. Fifth in birth order, he was aged forty and was born on the nineteenth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Boshun, his grandfather Yongzhao (posthumously appointed Director), and his father Fu (Right Provincial Administration Commissioner); his mother was née Yu (granted the title Lady). Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Hong (Prefectural School Instructor), Shao (Vice Director in the Ministry of Justice), Shou (Right Administration Vice Commissioner), and Shen. He married a woman née Huang. He placed twenty-seventh in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and fiftieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ge Yong, registered in Jiading County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Wenzhen. First in birth order, he was aged thirty-eight and was born on the sixth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Mao, his grandfather Ming (granted the privilege of wearing official cap and belt under provisions for imperial favor), and his father Fan; his mother was née Ma. His parents and grandparent or grandparents were living. His younger brothers were Fu and Yue. He married a woman née Jin. He placed twenty-seventh in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventy-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Zhang, registered in Fushi County, Yan'an Prefecture, Shaanxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Tingxian. First in birth order, he was aged thirty-eight and was born on the twenty-first day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Cheng, his grandfather Lin, and his father Yin; his mother was née Ma and his stepmother née Jia. His father was deceased and his mother was living. His younger brothers were Fu, Lu, and Xue. He married a woman née Dong. He placed fifteenth in the Shaan[□] [?] Provincial Examination and two hundred and first in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wang Zao, courtesy name Qizhao, was registered in a military household of Lin’an Guard, Yunnan, and was a native of Longquan County, Jiangxi. A student of the Lin’an Prefectural School, he specialized in the Book of Changes. He was first in birth order, aged twenty-seven, and born on the fourth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yongshou, his grandfather Xun, and his father Hong; his mother was née Jiang. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Kun, Hao, Bing, Chang, Yang, Dan, and Mian. His wife was née Fan. He ranked seventh in the Yunnan Provincial Examination and 133rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ye Luan, courtesy name Zhongxiu, was registered in a civilian household of Changshu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered region. An Imperial University student, he specialized in the Book of Odes. He was third in birth order, aged thirty-seven, and born on the twenty-first day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ziheng, his grandfather Shimao, and his father Gongxing; his mother was née Shi. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Yue and Yan. His wife was née Ping. He ranked seventy-sixth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 230th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Yizhen, courtesy name Ruzhen, was registered in a civilian household of Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian. An Imperial University student, he specialized in the Book of Odes. He was second in birth order, aged twenty-nine, and born on the twelfth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhizhong, an Assistant Magistrate; his grandfather was Chonghan [?], and his father Hongqi. His mother was née Xu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Yipei, and his younger brothers were Yigong, Yixian, and Yijiang. His wife was née Lin. He ranked seventeenth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 181st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sun Yan, courtesy name Shichang, was registered in an artisan household of Daxing County, Shuntian Prefecture, and was a native of Yuyao County, Zhejiang. An Imperial University student, he specialized in the Book of Rites. He was third in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the eighth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Quan, his grandfather Rixin, and his father Yi; his mother was née Zhang, and his stepmother née Yang. His parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Mao and Kan. He married a woman née Huang and was subsequently betrothed to a woman née Chen. He ranked 102nd in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 219th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xu Jie 許節, registered in a military household in Jiangxia County, Wuchang Prefecture, Huguang, was a National University student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Benjian; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged thirty-eight, born on the sixth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wengui; his grandfather, Mingde; his father, Congshan, an Assistant Prefect; and his mother, née Liu. His mother alone survived. His younger brothers were Cheng and Shen, and his wife was née Dai. He placed twenty-ninth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 276th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Shanyue 王山嶽, registered in a civilian household in Lingbi County, Suzhou Subprefecture, Fengyang Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a National University student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Xifu; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged thirty-four, born on the third day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhiyuan; his grandfather, Jingxin; his father, Ze, an Admonisher; his mother, née Fang; and his stepmother, née Wang. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Kunlun, and his wife was née Bao. He placed sixty-eighth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventy-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Long 張隆, registered in a military household in Xia County, Jiezhou Subprefecture, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, was a National University student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Shichang; he ranked third among his brothers and was aged thirty-four, born on the fourth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ximeng; his grandfather, Bin, posthumously granted the title of Secretary; his father, Heng; and his mother, née Zhao. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Chen and Lian, and his wife was née Chen. He placed fifth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 220th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qiu Tianyou 丘天祐, registered in a military household in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, was a Confucian scholar specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Hengji; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged twenty-eight, born on the twenty-ninth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shengyuan; his grandfather, Kongfu; his father, Zongmian; his legal mother, née Yu; and his birth mother, née Su. Both parents were living, and his wife was née Li. He placed seventeenth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 271st in the Metropolitan Examination.

His courtesy name was Sili; he was second in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the twenty-third day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Weiyi, his grandfather Rude, his father Zhang, and his mother Lady Song. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Zongfu, and his younger brothers were Zongbi and Zongzuo. He married Lady Guo. He ranked eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 210th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Dou Xiang, registered in Gong County, Henan Prefecture, Henan, in a military household, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Wenrui; he was first in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the twenty-third day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Cheng, his grandfather Zhong, his father Yue, and his mother Lady He. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Zhang. He married Lady Ding. He ranked sixty-second in the Henan Provincial Examination and 282nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Wen, registered in the Right Battalion of the Henan Guard in Henan, in a military household, was originally from Chao County in the directly administered region. He was a student of the Henan Prefectural School specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Daoxian; he was first in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the seventh day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Yulin, his grandfather Yi, his father Wang, and his mother Lady Zheng. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Jiao, Xuan, and Li. He married Lady Dong. He ranked twentieth in the Henan Provincial Examination and eighty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Ying, registered in Boye County, Baoding Prefecture, in the directly administered region, in a civilian household, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Dezhang; he was first in birth order, aged forty, and born on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Shi’an, his grandfather Xian, and his father Liang, a Prison Warden. His father's former wife was Lady Zhao, and his mother was Lady Xia. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Jie, a student of the Directorate of Education, and Xiong. He married Lady Ge. He ranked 208th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and sixty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

韓庭〔貫直隸真定府晉州民籍，國子生，治書經，字鳳集，行四，年四十，二月二十一日生〕。曾祖榮福，祖仲禮，父恭〔訓導〕，母雷氏。永感下，兄廣〔貢士〕、慶、廉，娶焦氏。順天府鄉試第三十八名，會試第一百六十五名。

高雲〔貫直隸淮安府山陽縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字從龍，行一，年四十一，五月二十六日生〕。曾祖士達，祖伯寧，父子敬，母夏氏。慈侍下，弟霦、岳，娶王氏。應天府鄉試第五十二名，會試第二百三十四名。

余璘〔貫直隸永平府灤州軍籍，廣德州人，國子生，治詩經，字德潤，行二，年四十五，正月二十五日生〕。曾祖慶，祖亨，父顯忠〔所大使〕，母杜氏。永感下，兄珉，娶張氏。順天府鄉試第九十七名，會試第二百七十五名。
translation_en:
Wei Ying, registered in a civilian household in Cixi County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, was an additional student of the county school specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Shihua, he was third in birth order, and he was aged twenty-three, born on the thirtieth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shangyuan, his grandfather Wen, his father Yuanji, and his mother née Feng; both parents were living, his elder brothers were Pa and Yi, his younger brothers Kui and Fang, and his wife was née Zhong; he placed fifteenth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and ninety-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Han Ting, registered in a civilian household in Jinzhou, Zhending Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Fengji, he was fourth in birth order, and he was aged forty, born on the twenty-first day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rongfu, his grandfather Zhongli, his father Gong (an Assistant Instructor), and his mother née Lei; both parents were deceased, his elder brothers were Guang (a tribute scholar), Qing, and Lian, and his wife was née Jiao; he placed thirty-eighth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 165th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Gao Yun, registered in a civilian household in Shanyang County, Huai’an Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Conglong, he was first in birth order, and he was aged forty-one, born on the twenty-sixth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shida, his grandfather Boning, his father Zijing, and his mother née Xia; his father was deceased and his mother living, his younger brothers were Bin and Yue, and his wife was née Wang; he placed fifty-second in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 234th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yu Lin, registered in a military household in Luanzhou, Yongping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and originally from Guangde Subprefecture, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Derun, he was second in birth order, and he was aged forty-five, born on the twenty-fifth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Qing, his grandfather Heng, his father Xianzhong (an Office Commissioner), and his mother née Du; both parents were deceased, his elder brother was Min, and his wife was née Zhang; he placed ninety-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 275th in the Metropolitan Examination.

李振綱〔貫河南開封府封丘縣，軍籍，縣學生，治書經，字廷憲，行一，年三十，閏九月初七日生〕。曾祖良，祖整，父和，母方氏。重慶下，弟振紀，娶馬氏。河南鄉試第六十七名，會試第一百五十三名。

常軏〔貫山西澤州沁水縣，民籍，國子生，治詩經，字時用，行四，年三十六，正月二十日生〕。曾祖君美，祖謙，父瑜〔倉大使〕，母楊氏。永感下，兄曇、懷、琪，娶萬氏。山西鄉試第十七名，會試第一百五十二名。
translation_en:
Zhang Zuan 張纘, registered in a civilian household in Huating County, Songjiang Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was an Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Tingsu, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-eight, born on the twenty-first day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Bin, his grandfather Xin, his father Xuan, and his mother Lady Zhu; both parents were living, his younger brother was Shen, and his wife was Lady Zhuang; he placed sixty-sixth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 223rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhou Qi 周琦, registered in a civilian household in Maping County, Liuzhou Prefecture, Guangxi, was an Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Changes; his courtesy name was Tingxi, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was aged forty-one, born on the twelfth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shiming, his grandfather Qingfu, his father Li, and his mother Lady Wu; his mother alone was living, his younger brothers were Zhen and Zhang, and he married Lady Qin and subsequently Lady Ou; he placed forty-third in the Guangxi Provincial Examination and 101st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Zhengang 李振綱, registered in a military household in Fengqiu County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, was a county government school student specializing in the Classic of Documents; his courtesy name was Tingxian, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was aged thirty, born on the seventh day of the intercalary ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Liang, his grandfather Zheng, his father He, and his mother Lady Fang; he had living grandparents and parents, his younger brother was Zhenji, and his wife was Lady Ma; he placed sixty-seventh in the Henan Provincial Examination and 153rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chang Yue 常軏, registered in a civilian household in Qinshui County, Zezhou Subprefecture, Shanxi, was an Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Shiyong, he ranked fourth among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-six, born on the twentieth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Junmei, his grandfather Qian, his father Yu (a granary commissioner), and his mother Lady Yang; both parents were deceased, his elder brothers were Tan, Huai, and Qi, and his wife was Lady Wan; he placed seventeenth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 152nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhao Luan 趙鑾 was registered in Jiangling County, Jingzhou Prefecture, Huguang, in a military household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Tingzhen and was first in birth order, aged twenty-nine, born on the twenty-sixth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wencai, his grandfather Li, and his father Yongqing (Granary Commissioner); his mother was née Li. His father was living and his mother deceased. He married a woman née Li. He ranked fifty-sixth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 299th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Yan 張閻 was registered in Kuaiji County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Zongwang and was second in birth order, aged forty-four, born on the twenty-fifth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Deli, his grandfather Youshan, and his father E; his mother was née Shao. Both parents were living. His elder brothers are listed as Tang, □, Wen, and Wangzhen [?; the names and their division are uncertain]. He married a woman née Zheng. He ranked forty-fourth [?; the character following the number is illegible] in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 273rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Jian 汪堅 was registered in Wuyuan County, Huizhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he had the courtesy name Shouzhen and was first in birth order, aged forty-six, born on the twenty-first day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Biao, his grandfather Tong, and his father Wei; his mother was née Cheng. Both parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers are listed as Yu, Tan, Shou, and Jun [?; the transcribed names are doubtful]. He married a woman née Cheng. He ranked sixty-first in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eightieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Lin 張琳 was registered in the Datong Left Guard, Shanxi, in a military household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Tingpei and was first in birth order, aged forty-three, born on the twenty-eighth day of the intercalary second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xiaoxian, his grandfather Rong, and his father Zheng; his mother was née Yao, and his stepmother née Tian. His father was deceased and his mother or stepmother living. His younger brother was Xuan. He married a woman née Shi. He ranked thirty-fifth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and ninety-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

黃珎〔貫順天府大興縣匠籍，浙江餘姚縣人，國子生，治禮記，字文瑞，行五，年三十三，三月初一日生〕。曾祖道昌，祖德受，父仕仁，嫡母沈氏，生母陳氏。具慶下，兄珉、珣、琳、琛，弟璘，娶熊氏。順天府鄉試第一百十六名，會試第一百五十四名。
translation_en:
Cui Zan 崔瓚, registered in a civilian household in Yizhou, Baoding Prefecture, in the directly administered region, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Zongqi; he was first in birth order, aged forty-four, and born on the tenth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wensheng, his grandfather Bingzhi, his father Lin, and his mother née Tian. Both parents were living. He married a woman née Liang and subsequently a woman née Liu. He ranked twenty-first in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 294th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wen Zhao 聞釗, registered in a civilian household in Changshu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered region, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Yuanming; he was third in birth order, aged thirty-five, and born on the eleventh day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhong, his grandfather Shiheng, his father Tingyan, and his mother née Wang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Jian, a District Magistrate, and Qin; his younger brother was Yue. He married a woman née Ping. He ranked 110th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 240th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Wo 鄭窩 [?], registered in a civilian household in Haiyang County, Chaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Tianmin; he was second in birth order, aged forty, and born on the seventeenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xuan, his grandfather Ren, and his father Qing, posthumously granted the title of Investigating Censor. His mother, née Li, was granted the title of Grand Lady of Respect. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother An was a Surveillance Vice Commissioner. He married a woman née Huang. He ranked thirty-sixth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 141st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Huang Zhen 黃珎, registered in an artisan household in Daxing County, Shuntian Prefecture, and originally from Yuyao County, Zhejiang, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Wenrui; he was fifth in birth order, aged thirty-three, and born on the first day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Daochang, his grandfather Deshou, and his father Shiren; his legal mother was née Shen and his birth mother née Chen. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Min, Xun, Lin 琳, and Chen; his younger brother was Lin 璘. He married a woman née Xiong. He ranked 116th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 154th in the Metropolitan Examination.

孔經〔貫福建邵武府邵武縣軍籍，府學生，治詩經，字大猷，行一，年二十七，五月十六日生〕。曾祖得清，祖章〔縣丞〕，父昭，母謝氏，繼母黃氏。具慶下，弟綸、紹、綱、縉、紳，娶王氏。福建鄉試第八十五名，會試第二百九十五名。

張鑑〔貫山東濟南府歷城縣民籍，國子生，治書經，字恒明，行二，年四十四，五月十八日生〕。曾祖思寧，祖銘，父俊〔縣丞〕，母史氏。永感下，兄鏞，弟鑄，娶李氏。山東鄉試第四十九名，會試第一百五十一名。

趙進〔貫河南開封府許州郾城縣民籍，國子生，治禮記，字藎之，行一，年二十九，十月十六日生〕。曾祖敬〔知府〕，祖鏞，父紘，母王氏。具慶下，弟逵、述、迪，娶張氏。河南鄉試第十名，會試第二百六十六名。

李澓〔貫河南開封府祥符縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字宗禹，行二，年三十三，六月初一日生〕。曾祖成，祖榮〔封監察御史〕，父芳，母晏氏。慈侍下，兄演，弟瀾、渥、源〔貢士〕、洪、浦，娶白氏，繼娶張氏。河南鄉試第七十三名，會試第二百十七名。
translation_en:
Kong Jing, registered in a military household in Shaowu County, Shaowu Prefecture, Fujian, was a prefectural school student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Dayou; he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-seven years old, born on the sixteenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Deqing; his grandfather, Zhang, was a county vice magistrate; his father was Zhao; his mother was née Xie, and his stepmother was née Huang. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Lun, Shao, Gang, Jin, and Shen. He married a woman née Wang. He placed eighty-fifth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 295th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Jian, registered in a civilian household in Licheng County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Documents. His courtesy name was Hengming; he ranked second among his brothers and was forty-four years old, born on the eighteenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Sining; his grandfather was Ming; his father, Jun, was a county vice magistrate; and his mother was née Shi. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Yong, and his younger brother was Zhu. He married a woman née Li. He placed forty-ninth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 151st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhao Jin, registered in a civilian household in Yancheng County, Xuzhou Subprefecture, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Record of Rites. His courtesy name was Jinzhi; he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-nine years old, born on the sixteenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather, Jing, was a prefect; his grandfather was Yong; his father was Hong; and his mother was née Wang. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Kui, Shu, and Di. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed tenth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 266th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Fu, registered in a civilian household in Xiangfu County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Zongyu; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-three years old, born on the first day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Cheng; his grandfather, Rong, had been granted the honorary title of investigating censor; his father was Fang; and his mother was née Yan. His mother was living, and his father was deceased. His elder brother was Yan; his younger brothers were Lan, Wo, Yuan (a tribute scholar), Hong, and Pu. He married a woman née Bai and subsequently a woman née Zhang. He placed seventy-third in the Henan Provincial Examination and 217th in the Metropolitan Examination.

崔巖〔貫湖廣郴州，民籍，州學生，治易經，字民瞻，行一，年二十六，十月初四日生〕。曾祖禎〔長史〕，祖綱〔倉大使，贈經歷〕，父鑑〔京衛經歷〕，母戴氏〔封孺人〕。重慶下，娶王氏。湖廣鄉試第四十八名，會試第一百八十名。

張昪〔貫直隸大名府開州長垣縣，民籍，縣學生，治詩經，字孟昭，行三，年三十一，正月十九日生〕。曾祖進，祖亨，父璁〔教授〕，母黃氏，繼母許氏。永感下，兄旻、冕〔知縣〕，弟昇、昺、曇、景、暴、暠，娶焦氏。順天府鄉試第一百二十一名，會試第十名。

徐智〔貫山東東昌府濮州范縣，民籍，國子生，治詩經，字景哲，行三，年四十一，二月初二日生〕。曾祖二，祖文義，父良，母楊氏，繼母劉氏、昝氏。具慶下，兄聰、睿，娶高氏，繼娶趙氏。山東鄉試第六十九名，會試第一百三十七名。

曲銳〔貫山東登州府萊陽縣，軍籍，縣學生，治書經，字朝儀，行一，年二十五，六月十五日生〕。曾祖名禮，祖從，父敬，母劉氏，繼母初氏。具慶下，弟𨦣，娶趙氏。山東鄉試第六十六名，會試第一百四十七名。
translation_en:
Cui Yan, registered in Chenzhou, Huguang, belonged to a civilian household and was a prefectural government school student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Minzhan; he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-six years old, born on the fourth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhen, Chief Administrator; his grandfather was Gang, Granary Commissioner, posthumously awarded the title of Registrar; his father was Jian, Registrar of a capital guard; and his mother, née Dai, was granted the title of Lady (ruren). His grandparents and parents were living. He married a woman née Wang. He placed forty-eighth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 180th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Bian, registered in Changyuan County, Kaizhou, Daming Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a county government school student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Mengzhao; he ranked third among his brothers and was thirty-one years old, born on the nineteenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jin; his grandfather, Heng; his father, Cong, a Prefectural School Instructor; his mother was née Huang, and his stepmother née Xu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Min and Mian, the latter a District Magistrate; his younger brothers were Sheng, Bing, Tan, Jing, Bao, and Gao. He married a woman née Jiao. He placed 121st in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and tenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Zhi, registered in Fan County, Puzhou, Dongchang Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a civilian household and was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Jingzhe; he ranked third among his brothers and was forty-one years old, born on the second day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Er; his grandfather, Wenyi; and his father, Liang. His mother was née Yang, and his successive stepmothers were née Liu and née Zan. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Cong and Rui. He married a woman née Gao and subsequently a woman née Zhao. He placed sixty-ninth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 137th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qu Rui, registered in Laiyang County, Dengzhou Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a military household and was a county government school student specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Chaoyi; he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-five years old, born on the fifteenth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Mingli; his grandfather, Cong; and his father, Jing. His mother was née Liu, and his stepmother née Chu. Both parents were living. His younger brother’s name is transcribed as 𨦣 [?]. He married a woman née Zhao. He placed sixty-sixth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 147th in the Metropolitan Examination.

郭緒〔貫河南開封府太康縣，民籍，縣學生，治書經，字繼業，行二，年三十七，六月初七日生〕。曾祖在豐〔知縣〕，祖浩，父杲，前母符氏，母楊氏。永感下，兄統，弟紀，娶彭氏。河南鄉試第七十二名，會試第一百七十九名。

王佑〔貫山東濟南府肥城縣，民籍，國子生，治詩經，字廷佐，行四，年四十一，二月二十四日生〕。曾祖新，祖士賢，父敬，前母李氏，母趙氏。永感下，兄義、禮、智，弟信，娶朱氏。山東鄉試第二十一名，會試第二百三十二名。
translation_en:
Guo Bingzhao, registered in Guiyang County, Chenzhou, Huguang, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Wenhui, he ranked fifth among his brothers, and he was aged forty-one, born on the eleventh day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Shikui, his grandfather Zhimin, and his father Run, a County Vice Magistrate; his father's former wife was née He, and his mother was née Luo. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Bingji, Binggang, Bingtong, and Bingyao, and his younger brother was Bingke; his wife was née He. He placed thirteenth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and forty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ma Xiang, registered in Tongzhou, Xi'an Prefecture, Shaanxi, belonged to an artisan household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Changes; his courtesy name was Wenrui, he ranked second among his brothers, and he was aged forty-one, born on the eighteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Kezhong, his grandfather Can, his father Ying, and his mother née Dong. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brother was Sheng and his younger brother Zhen; his wife was née Che. He placed thirty-sixth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 227th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Xu, registered in Taikang County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, belonged to a civilian household and was a county school student specializing in the Classic of Documents; his courtesy name was Jiye, he ranked second among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-seven, born on the seventh day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Zaifeng, a County Magistrate, his grandfather Hao, and his father Gao; his father's former wife was née Fu, and his mother was née Yang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Tong and his younger brother Ji; his wife was née Peng. He placed seventy-second in the Henan Provincial Examination and 179th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang You, registered in Feicheng County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Tingzuo, he ranked fourth among his brothers, and he was aged forty-one, born on the twenty-fourth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Xin, his grandfather Shixian, and his father Jing; his father's former wife was née Li, and his mother was née Zhao. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Yi, Li, and Zhi, and his younger brother was Xin; his wife was née Zhu. He placed twenty-first in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 232nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

張佐〔貫湖廣黃州衛軍籍，直隸廣德州人，國子生，治詩經，字良弼，行一，年三十六，九月初四日生〕。曾祖顯二，祖伯昌，父福，母丁氏，繼母李氏。具慶下，弟儀，娶聞氏。湖廣鄉試第六十七名，會試第七十四名。

王純〔貫浙江台州府僊居縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字弘文，行二，年四十八，七月二十七日生〕。曾祖嗣宗〔訓科〕，祖原行，父懷廣，母顧氏。永感下，兄弘學，弟弘榦、弘度、弘範，娶張氏。應天府鄉試第八十八名，會試第一百八名。

曹佺〔貫湖廣郴州永興縣民籍，國子生，治禮記，字存之，行三，年四十二，六月初十日生〕。曾祖永益，祖受聰〔典史〕，父璉〔大理寺左少卿〕，前母李氏，母華氏。慈侍下，兄仕〔國子生〕、儒〔義官〕，弟倬〔義官〕、儀〔貢士〕，娶李氏，繼娶顏氏。湖廣鄉試第十名，會試第二百二十九名。

耿瑛〔貫河南開封府杞縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字玉光，行一，年四十，四月初十日生〕。曾祖思義，祖得林，父欽，母馬氏，繼母孔氏。具慶下，弟瑜、珣〔省祭官〕、珎〔聽選官〕、琬，娶王氏。河南鄉試第三十八名，會試第三百八十一名。
translation_en:
Zhang Zuo, courtesy name Liangbi, was registered in a military household of Huangzhou Guard, Huguang, and was a native of Guangde Subprefecture in Zhili. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was the eldest son, aged thirty-six, and born on the fourth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Xian’er; his grandfather, Bochang; and his father, Fu. His mother was née Ding and his stepmother née Li. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Yi, and his wife was née Wen. He ranked sixty-seventh in the Huguang Provincial Examination and seventy-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Chun, courtesy name Hongwen, was registered in a civilian household in Xianju County, Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was the second son, aged forty-eight, and born on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Sizong, a Medical Instructor; his grandfather, Yuanxing; and his father, Huaiguang. His mother was née Gu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Hongxue, and his younger brothers were Honggan, Hongdu, and Hongfan. His wife was née Zhang. He ranked eighty-eighth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and one hundred eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cao Quan, courtesy name Cunzhi, was registered in a civilian household in Yongxing County, Chenzhou Subprefecture, Huguang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Rites, he was the third son, aged forty-two, and born on the tenth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Yongyi; his grandfather, Shoucong, an Unranked Miscellaneous Official; and his father, Lian, Left Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review. His father's former wife was née Li, and his mother was née Hua. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Shi, an Imperial University student, and Ru, an Honorary Official for Philanthropy; his younger brothers were Zhuo, also an Honorary Official for Philanthropy, and Yi, a tribute scholar. His wife was née Li; he subsequently married a woman née Yan. He ranked tenth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and two hundred twenty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Geng Ying, courtesy name Yuguang, was registered in a civilian household in Qi County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was the eldest son, aged forty, and born on the tenth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Siyi; his grandfather, Delin; and his father, Qin. His mother was née Ma and his stepmother née Kong. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yu; Xun, a sacrificial attendant (shengjiguan); Zhen, an official awaiting selection for appointment; and Wan. His wife was née Wang. He ranked thirty-eighth in the Henan Provincial Examination and three hundred eighty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en: Jiang Ying 蔣濙 was registered in Shangrao County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi, in a military household. He was a student of the Directorate of Education and specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Zichuan. He was first in birth order, aged thirty-seven, and born on the third day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Jianshan; his grandfather, Yi, served as a District Magistrate; his father was Shikui, and his mother was née Xu. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Pan, a tribute scholar (gongshi), Si, and Wen. His wife was née Xu. He ranked forty-eighth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and eighty-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰朕祗奉丕
圖究惟化理欲追
三代以底雍熈不
可不求定論焉夫
三代之王天下必
===
有紀綱法度然後
可以言治而議者
乃謂三代之治在
道不在法豈法無
所用乎聖王立法

translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: “Reverently upholding the great imperial enterprise, I ponder deeply the principles of governance and moral transformation. Desiring to emulate the Three Dynasties and attain harmony and prosperity, I must seek a definitive judgment on this matter. Now, when the Three Dynasties ruled All under Heaven, they necessarily had governing principles and laws and institutions; only then could there be talk of good government. Yet commentators maintain that the good government of the Three Dynasties lay in the Way, rather than in laws. Could laws, then, have served no purpose? When the sage kings established laws…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
必有名以表實然
後可以傳遠而議
者乃謂三代之法
貴實不貴名豈名
非所先乎治不在
===
法則繼以仁政之
說似戾法不貴名
則必也正名之說
似迂二者將何所
從也嗣是稱治者

===
法則繼以仁政之
說似矣法不貴名
則必也正名之說
似迂二者將何所
從也嗣是稱治者
punctuated: 必有名以表實，然後可以傳遠。而議者乃謂三代之法貴實不貴名，豈名非所先乎？治不在法，則繼以仁政之說似戾；法不貴名，則必也正名之說似迂。二者將何所從也？嗣是稱治者，
translation_en: …there must be names to express the substance; only then can the laws be transmitted to distant generations. Yet commentators maintain that the laws of the Three Dynasties valued substance rather than names. Surely names must come first? If good government does not reside in laws, then the saying that one must follow them with benevolent government seems contradictory; if laws do not value names, then the saying that one must first rectify names seems far-fetched. Which of these two positions should one follow? Among those celebrated for good government thereafter…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
莫過於漢唐宋漢
大綱正於父子君
臣之道蓋得矣而
其治何以不能繼
夫周七制之君知
===
===
重道者孰優乎唐
萬目舉如田賦兵
刑之法近實矣而
其治何以不相遠
於漢三宗之內能
alt_text:
莫過於漢唐宋漢
大綱正於父子君
臣之道蓋得矣而
其治何以不能繼
夫周七制之君知
===
重道者孰優乎唐
萬目舉如田賦兵
刑之法近實矣而
其治何以不相遠
於漢三宋之明能
punctuated: 莫過於漢唐宋。漢大綱正，於父子君臣之道蓋得矣，而其治何以不能繼夫周？七制之君，知重道者孰優乎？唐萬目舉，如田賦兵刑之法近實矣，而其治何以不相遠於漢？三宗之內，能
translation_en: …none surpassed the Han, Tang, and Song. Under the Han, the cardinal principles were set right, and the proper relations between father and son and between ruler and minister were apparently grasped. Yet why could its governance not match that of the Zhou? Among the rulers of the seven reigns, which best understood the importance of the Way? Under the Tang, the manifold particulars of administration were put into effect: such regulations as those governing land taxes, military affairs, and punishments approached practical substance. Yet why did its governance differ so little from that of the Han? Among the three ancestral emperors, who was able to…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
守法者孰賢乎至
宋則大綱正萬目
未盡舉似於唐不
及然又謂其家法
有遠過漢唐足以
===
===
致太平者八事而
并指其君之賢其
說又何所據也夫
法不徒行名不苟
立古之人必有處
alt_text:
守法者孰賢乎至
宗則大綱正萬目
未盡舉似於唐不
及然又謂其家法
有遠過漢唐是以
===
致太平者八事而
并稽其君之賢其
說又何所據也夫
法不徒行名不苟
立古之人必有處
punctuated: 守法者孰賢乎？至宋，則大綱正，萬目未盡舉，似於唐不及；然又謂其家法有遠過漢唐、足以致太平者八事，而并指其君之賢，其說又何所據也？夫法不徒行，名不苟立，古之人必有處
translation_en: …who was the worthiest in upholding the laws? Coming to the Song, its principal framework was sound, but its myriad particulars were not fully implemented, seemingly leaving it inferior to the Tang. Yet it is also said that eight features of its dynastic institutions far surpassed those of the Han and Tang and were sufficient to bring about great peace; the worthiness of its rulers is also singled out. On what grounds, then, do these claims rest? Laws do not operate of themselves, nor are reputations established without grounds. The ancients must have had some basis for their conduct…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
乎此者而後世獲
效之不同如彼何
也兹朕於道必欲
探其精微之蘊於
法必欲參其制作
===
之詳於所謂名與
實者必欲考求三
代之所以相須而
治漢唐宋之所以
不相須而治不古
alt_text:
乎此者而後世獲
效之不同如彼何
也茲朕於道必欲
探其精微之藴於
法必欲參其制作
===
之詳於所謂名與
實者必欲考稽三
代之所以相須而
治漢唐宋之所以
不相須而治不古
punctuated: 乎此者，而後世獲效之不同如彼，何也？兹朕於道，必欲探其精微之蘊；於法，必欲參其制作之詳；於所謂名與實者，必欲考求三代之所以相須而治，漢唐宋之所以不相須而治不古
translation_en: …in this matter; yet later generations obtained such different results. Why was this? Now, regarding the Way, I wish to probe its subtle and profound meaning; regarding institutions, I wish to examine the details of their establishment. As for what are called names and realities, I wish to investigate why these supported one another under the Three Dynasties and brought about good government, and why under the Han, Tang, and Song they did not support one another, and government did not equal that of antiquity…

text:
善者庶幾取舍明
而躋世雍熈可期
也諸生學古通今
出膺時用必審知
之矣其各殫心以
===
對毋略毋泛朕將
采而行焉
成化十七年三月十五日

著者庶幾取僉明
而躋世雍熙可期
也諸生學古通今
出膺時用必審知
之矣其各殫心以
===
對毋略毋泛朕將
采而行焉
成化十七年三月十五日
punctuated:
善者，庶幾取舍明，而躋世雍熈可期也。諸生學古通今，出膺時用，必審知之矣。其各殫心以對，毋略毋泛，朕將采而行焉。
成化十七年三月十五日。
translation_en:
…as well governed as in antiquity, in the hope that the choices of what to adopt and what to reject may become clear, and that bringing the world to harmony and prosperity may be within reach. You students have studied antiquity and understand the present; as you come forth to serve the needs of the age, you must surely understand these matters thoroughly. Let each of you devote his utmost thought to his reply. Be neither cursory nor vague. I shall select from your proposals and put them into practice.
The fifteenth day of the third month of the seventeenth year of Chenghua (1481).

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
臣王華
臣對臣聞人君之治天下有體焉有用焉體者何道
是也用者何法是也道原於天而不可易所以根柢
乎法者也法因乎時而制其宜所以品節乎道者也
道立而法未備則民生未遂民患未除未足以言治
法具而道未立則綱常淪斁風俗頹靡又奚足以為
治哉故善為治者不徒恃乎法以制天下之人要必
本於道而善為法者不徒徇乎名以誣天下之人要
必求其實焉夏商周之所以致天下於大治者以其
有得乎此也漢唐宋之所以治不古若者以其胥失
===
乎此也然則
今日欲究化理而求定論亦惟遵三王之道行三王之
法務使全體大用之畢舉而陋漢唐宋於不為可也
豈必外此而他求哉書曰監于先王成憲其永無愆
此之謂也欽惟
皇帝陛下睿知聰明根於天性寛仁莊敬見於躬行丕承
一祖四宗之鴻圖默契二帝三王之心學涵養深而天理
明歷閱久而世故熟是以十有八年之間
聖德日新治效日隆誠可謂
大有為之君不世出之主也然猶不自滿假迺於

Your servant Wang Hua.
Your servant replies: I have heard that the ruler’s governance of All under Heaven has both a substance and a functioning. What is its substance? The Way. What is its functioning? Institutions. The Way originates in Heaven and cannot be altered; it provides the foundation for institutions. Institutions are adapted to the times and fashioned to suit their circumstances; they give measured expression to the Way. If the Way is established but institutions are incomplete, the people’s livelihood remains unfulfilled and their afflictions unrelieved: this is insufficient to be called good government. If institutions are complete but the Way is not established, the cardinal relationships and constant moral norms fall into ruin, and customs deteriorate: how, then, can this count as good government? Thus, one skilled in governing does not merely rely on institutions to regulate the people of the realm, but must ground government in the Way. One skilled in devising institutions does not merely pursue names to deceive the people of the realm, but must seek their substance. The Xia, Shang, and Zhou brought All under Heaven to excellent order because they grasped this. The Han, Tang, and Song failed to match the government of antiquity because they all missed it. If, then, we wish today to investigate moral transformation and good government and reach a settled judgment, we need only follow the Way of the Three Kings and implement their institutions, ensuring that the whole substance and its great functioning are fully realized, while rejecting the practices of the Han, Tang, and Song as unworthy of imitation. Why seek elsewhere? The Book of Documents says: “Look to the established statutes of the former kings, and you will forever be without error.” This is what it means.
I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor’s sagacity and discernment are rooted in your heavenly endowment, while your magnanimity, benevolence, dignity, and reverence manifest themselves in your personal conduct. You have grandly inherited the great dynastic enterprise of the one founding ancestor and four ancestral emperors, and inwardly accord with the learning of the mind of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. Through profound self-cultivation, heavenly principle is clear to you; through long experience, you are thoroughly acquainted with worldly affairs. Thus, over these eighteen years, your sacred virtue has been renewed daily, and the achievements of your government have grown daily more splendid. Truly, you may be called a ruler of great accomplishments, a sovereign rarely seen in any age. Yet you remain free of self-satisfaction, and so, during …

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
幾之暇
埀集諸生諏咨治道且欲求一定之論以追三代之隆
臣有以知
陛下是心其即古帝王好問好察謀及士庶之心也臣以
草茅之微獲與諸生之列仰承
明詔敢不俯竭愚忠茂明
大對以少裨萬分之一乎臣竊惟治之體本於道治之
用存乎法法之行必有其名而名之立必有其實人
君所以持一定之論而致雍熈之治者端在於斯矣
且道莫大於綱常法莫大於田賦兵刑三綱不正不
===
足以言道四事不舉不足以語法臣請先以家喻之
今有鉅室焉父慈而子孝夫義而婦聽其家道正矣
然而耕耨失其時收斂無其術仰不足以事父母俯
不足以畜妻子或門庭之寇不能禦或奴隷之肆無
所懲如此而謂之家齊不可也其或家給人足令行
禁止而父子夫婦之間或有所歉如此而謂之家齊
不可也又或事事而為之名以聳人之觀聽而求其
實則泯然無蹟之可舉如此而謂之家齊可乎家之
於天下勢不同而理同道也法也實也名也誠可相
有而不可相無也昔者三代之王天下蓋有法以輔

於天下勢不同而理同道也法也實也名也誠可相
有而不可相無也昔者三代之王天下蓋有法以輔
punctuated:
幾之暇，埀集諸生，諏咨治道，且欲求一定之論，以追三代之隆。臣有以知陛下是心，其即古帝王好問好察、謀及士庶之心也。臣以草茅之微，獲與諸生之列，仰承明詔，敢不俯竭愚忠，茂明大對，以少裨萬分之一乎？臣竊惟治之體本於道，治之用存乎法。法之行必有其名，而名之立必有其實。人君所以持一定之論而致雍熈之治者，端在於斯矣。且道莫大於綱常，法莫大於田賦兵刑。三綱不正，不足以言道；四事不舉，不足以語法。
臣請先以家喻之。今有鉅室焉，父慈而子孝，夫義而婦聽，其家道正矣。然而耕耨失其時，收斂無其術，仰不足以事父母，俯不足以畜妻子；或門庭之寇不能禦，或奴隷之肆無所懲。如此而謂之家齊，不可也。其或家給人足，令行禁止，而父子夫婦之間或有所歉，如此而謂之家齊，不可也。又或事事而為之名，以聳人之觀聽，而求其實，則泯然無蹟之可舉。如此而謂之家齊，可乎？家之於天下，勢不同而理同。道也，法也，實也，名也，誠可相有而不可相無也。
昔者三代之王天下，蓋有法以輔
translation_en:
…in the intervals between affairs of state, you graciously assembled the scholars to consult them about the way of governing, seeking also a settled judgment by which to recover the flourishing rule of the Three Dynasties. Your servant can thus see that Your Majesty’s intention is precisely that of the ancient sage emperors and kings, who delighted in asking questions and examining matters closely, and extended their consultations to scholars and commoners. Though merely an insignificant man from the countryside, your servant has been permitted to join the ranks of these scholars and respectfully receive your enlightened edict. How could I fail to exert my humble loyalty to the utmost and fully expound my answer to this great inquiry, hoping to contribute even one part in ten thousand?
Your servant humbly considers that the substance of government is rooted in the Way, while its practical operation lies in institutions and laws. Their implementation must have corresponding names, and established names must have corresponding realities. It is precisely here that the ruler’s means of maintaining a settled judgment and achieving harmonious, flourishing government lie. In the Way, nothing is greater than the cardinal bonds and constant virtues; in institutions and laws, nothing is greater than land administration, taxation, military affairs, and punishments. If the three cardinal bonds are not properly ordered, one cannot speak of the Way; if these four affairs are not carried out, one cannot speak of institutions and laws.
Let your servant first illustrate this through a household. Suppose there is a great household in which the father is loving and the son filial, the husband righteous and the wife obedient: its domestic relationships are properly ordered. Yet if plowing and weeding miss their seasons and harvesting and storing lack proper methods, there will be insufficient means to support parents above or maintain wife and children below. Perhaps robbers at the gate cannot be repelled, or the insolence of servants goes unpunished. To call such a household well regulated would be impossible. Alternatively, even if the household is well supplied and everyone has enough, commands are carried out and prohibitions observed, yet something is lacking in the relationships between father and son or husband and wife, it would likewise be impossible to call that household well regulated. Or suppose impressive names are devised for every undertaking to dazzle people’s eyes and ears, yet when one seeks the reality behind them, there is not a trace to be found. Could such a household be called well regulated? A household and the realm differ in their circumstances, but share the same principles. The Way, institutions and laws, realities, and names must indeed coexist; none can dispense with the others.
In antiquity, when the rulers of the Three Dynasties ruled the realm, they had institutions and laws to assist…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
其治非專恃乎法也其立法也盖有名以表其實非
徒徇乎名也臣請略舉其槩如咸則三壤以制井田
差為九等以定貢賦六師以征不序三千而有贖條
此有夏治天下之法也八家各授一區以為私田八
家同養公田以給賦税設六軍之制制風愆之刑此
有商治天下之法也詳之為井牧溝洫而田有所分
纖之為九府圜法而賦有所統司馬掌九伐之法以
正邦國司寇掌五刑之制以糾萬民非成周治天下
之法乎其制田賦也實足以裕民而足國其制兵刑
也實足以禦亂而禁奸豈徒為虛名而已哉矧禹之
===
治本於祗台德先而率由典常則其法有道以為之
體故能文命誕敷以臻聲教四被之治湯之治本於
克寬克仁而肇脩人紀則其法有道以為之體故能
表正萬邦以成兆民允懷之治文王純亦不已而兹
迪彝教武王建其有極而重民五教則周之法亦有
道以為之體此所以致有夏脩和四海永清之治也
宋儒羅從彥謂三代之治在道不在法三代之法貴
實不貴名盖言法之不可以離道名之不可以失實
耳夫豈謂法無所用而名非所先乎三代而後稱善
治者莫過於漢唐宋若秦隋五季之流皆無足齒矣

translation_en:
…their government; they did not rely exclusively on laws. In establishing laws, they used names to express substantive realities, rather than merely pursuing names. Your servant asks leave to outline a few examples. They followed the characteristics of the three types of soil in establishing well-field allotments, distinguished nine grades to determine tribute and taxation, deployed six armies to chastise the disorderly, and provided rules for redemption among the three thousand penal provisions. These were the laws by which the Xia governed All under Heaven. Each of eight households received one plot as its private field, and all eight jointly cultivated the public field to supply taxes. A system of six armies was established, together with punishments for the faults of dissolute conduct. These were the laws by which the Shang governed All under Heaven. Fields were apportioned through detailed arrangements for well-field divisions, pastoral tracts, and drainage channels; revenues were brought under unified control through the intricate arrangements [?] of the nine treasuries and monetary regulations. The Minister of War administered the rules for nine kinds of punitive expedition to correct the states; the Minister of Justice administered the system of five punishments to discipline the myriad people. Were these not the laws by which the Zhou governed All under Heaven? Their provisions for fields and taxation were substantively sufficient to enrich the people and supply the state; their provisions for armies and punishments were substantively sufficient to repel disorder and restrain wrongdoing. How could these have been merely empty names?

Moreover, Yu’s government was rooted in the principle, “Reverently place my virtue first,” and followed established norms. Thus his laws had the Way as their substance, enabling his civilizing influence to spread widely and bringing about a government whose moral instruction reached in all four directions. Tang’s government was rooted in generosity and benevolence, and he began by putting human relationships in order. Thus his laws had the Way as their substance, enabling him to serve as a model and rectify the myriad states, and bringing about a government to which the multitude sincerely gave their allegiance. King Wen’s purity was unceasing, and he guided the people through enduring teachings. King Wu established the supreme standard and attached importance to the five teachings governing human relationships. Thus the laws of the Zhou likewise had the Way as their substance. This was how they achieved a government under which the Xia lands were brought into harmony and all within the Four Seas enjoyed lasting peace.

The Song Confucian scholar Luo Congyan said, “The government of the Three Dynasties lay in the Way, not in laws; the laws of the Three Dynasties valued substance, not names.” He meant only that laws cannot be separated from the Way, and that names cannot lose their substance. How could he have meant that laws serve no purpose, or that names need not receive prior attention? Among those praised for good government after the Three Dynasties, none surpassed the Han, Tang, and Song. As for the likes of the Qin, Sui, and Five Dynasties, none merits mention.

text:
漢高祖用三老之言而發義帝之喪赦季布之罪而
戮丁公之叛則君臣之義以明因家令之言而尊禮
太公高四皓之名而割愛衽席則父子之倫無失是
大綱正而道得其槩矣惜乎規模雖宏遠而多襲嬴
秦之舊詩書之不事而未脫馬上之習故其時去成
周雖未甚遠而田賦兵刑之類多缺典矣果能如三
代之治道法兼資者乎漢有天下歷年四百高祖而
下若文帝之躬脩玄默武帝之雄才大畧宣帝之信
賞必罰光武之沉幾先物明帝之遵𡬶成憲章帝之
寬厚長者亦皆一世之賢君王通取之為七制宜矣
===

之遺意定上中下府兵之制五覆奏三訊之刑依稀
乎先王兵刑之舊規是萬目舉而法近乎實矣惜乎
制度雖益詳而不能自身推之於家紀綱雖益密而

translation_en:
Gaozu of Han followed the advice of an elder and proclaimed mourning for Emperor Yi; he pardoned Ji Bu’s crime but executed Ding Gong for his treachery, thereby making clear the proper obligations between ruler and minister. Following the advice of the Household Administrator, he honored his father, the Grand Sire, with due ceremony; esteeming the reputation of the Four Hoary Elders, he relinquished his preference for his bedchamber favorite, thereby preserving the proper relationship between father and son. Thus the cardinal principles were set right, and the Way was grasped in its broad outlines. Regrettably, although his overall design was expansive and far-reaching, he retained much of the legacy of Qin under the Ying house. He neglected the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents and had not shed the habits of ruling from horseback. Consequently, although his time was not yet very distant from the age of Chengzhou, many proper institutions concerning land, taxation, military affairs, and punishments were lacking. Could this truly compare with the government of the Three Dynasties, which drew upon both the Way and institutional methods? The Han possessed the realm for four hundred years. From Gaozu onward, Emperor Wen personally cultivated profound quietude; Emperor Wu possessed outstanding ability and grand strategic vision; Emperor Xuan made rewards trustworthy and punishments certain; Guangwu discerned incipient developments with depth and anticipated events; Emperor Ming followed established statutes; and Emperor Zhang was generous and kind, like a venerable elder. All were worthy rulers of their age. Wang Tong was right to select them as the Seven Reigns. Yet, judged by their esteem for the Way, they appear never to have heard of the sages’ and worthies’ Way of the Great Learning. Your servant dares not pronounce with certainty which of them was superior. This is why Han government never surpassed the level of Han.

Taizong of Tang instituted land allotments held for life and land held as hereditary property, together with the system of grain tax, labor service or its commutation, and tax in textiles. These bore some resemblance to the intentions underlying the former kings’ arrangements for land and taxation. He established the system of militia commands graded upper, middle, and lower, and penal procedures requiring five memorials for review and three inquiries. These faintly resembled the former kings’ established rules for military affairs and punishments. Thus the myriad particulars were put into effect, and institutional methods approached substantive reality. Regrettably, although the institutions became more detailed, he could not extend their principles from himself to his family; although the framework of governance became more closely ordered, he could not extend it from his family to the state. Hence, although his institutional methods seemed to surpass those of the Former and Later Han, his conduct in the relationships between father and son and ruler and minister gave much cause for shame. Could this truly compare with the institutions of the Three Dynasties, in which name and substance sustained one another? The Tang possessed the realm through twenty reigns. After Taizong, Xuanzong quelled internal troubles, devoted himself energetically to government, and nearly achieved great peace; Xianzong was firm, discerning, and decisive, and able to make use of loyal …

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
謀克除僭叛亦皆繼世之令主史臣詠之為三宗當
矣然以守法言之則二帝三王之法邈乎其未之能
及臣未敢必其為孰賢此唐之治所以止於唐也逮
宋室之興太祖開基事周后如母愛少帝如子鞭朴
不施於殿陛罵辱不及於公卿慈闈一言載在金匱
舍子立弟付託得人其大綱可謂正矣但其兵雖有
三衙四廂之制而不足以禦外侮刑雖有折杖常刑
之典而不足以禁奸吏天下之田雖二十稅一而未
能合乎井牧溝洫之制役民之法雖因乎唐制而未
若租庸調法之詳其萬目則未盡舉也夫大綱雖正
===

臣妾之禮見仁宗以姪事姑此事長之法也前代宮

多預政事本朝不許預事此待外戚之法也前代宮

translation_en:
…counsel and successfully eliminating usurpers and rebels: these too were excellent rulers who inherited the throne. The historians were right to celebrate them as the Three Zong. Yet, in upholding established institutions, they remained far from attaining those of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. Your servant would not venture to determine which of them was worthier. This is why Tang government never rose beyond the level of the Tang.
When the Song house arose, Taizu laid its foundations. He served the empress of the Zhou as his mother and cherished its young emperor as his son. Whips and rods were not applied in the palace precincts, nor were insults directed at dukes and high ministers. A pronouncement of the empress dowager was recorded and kept in a golden coffer: passing over his son to enthrone his younger brother, he entrusted the succession to a suitable man. His principal framework may thus be called correct. Yet although his military organization had the system of the Three Commands and Four Divisions, it could not repel foreign aggression. Although his penal statutes provided for commutation to strokes of the heavy bamboo and for regular punishments, they could not restrain corrupt officials. Although the empire’s farmland was taxed at one part in twenty, its organization did not accord with the well-field and pastoral system and its irrigation channels and ditches. Although the regulations for imposing labor service followed Tang institutions, they were less detailed than the Tang system of grain tax, labor service or its commutation, and payment in textiles. The myriad particulars had therefore not all been put into effect. Though the principal framework was correct, the failure to implement all these particulars seems to place the Song below the Tang. Yet the excellence of its dynastic household rules surpassed those of the Han and Tang.
Lü Dafang once said: “In former dynasties, rulers paid their respects to their empress mothers at set times; since our dynastic ancestors, they have done so every morning and evening. This is the rule for serving one’s parents. In former dynasties, senior grand princesses appeared at court with the ceremonial deference of female subjects; Renzong served his aunt as a nephew. This is the rule for serving one’s elders. In former dynasties, the inner palace often lacked discipline; in our dynasty, the palace restrictions are strict. This is the rule for governing the inner household. In former dynasties, imperial relatives by marriage often participated in government; our dynasty does not permit them to take part. This is the rule for treating imperial relatives by marriage. In former dynasties, palaces commonly prized splendor and extravagance; our dynasty’s palace buildings use only red and white. This is the rule for esteeming frugality. In former dynasties, rulers used sedan chairs and carriages whenever they went about within the palace; our dynastic ancestors walked from the inner court to hold audience in the rear hall. This is the rule for exercising the body. In former dynasties, rulers were careless and informal in their headgear and dress within the palace; since our dynastic ancestors, even private leisure has invariably conformed to ritual propriety. This is the rule for esteeming ritual. Former dynasties were often renowned for severity in applying punishments [?]; only…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
本朝臣下有罪止於廢黜此寬仁之法也凡此八事
信乎家法之過漢唐矣太祖而下如太宗之恭儉好
文真宗之寬仁慈愛仁宗之力行恭儉英宗之優禮
大臣庶幾其賢者歟惜其仁厚有餘而剛斷不足此
宋之治亦止於宋而已夫法非自行必本於道而後
行名非自立必有其實而後立古之人皆有以處乎
此而後世獲效之不古若豈非以其或有體而無用
或有用而無體歟洪惟我
