本朝臣下有罪，止於廢黜，此寬仁之法也。凡此八事，信乎家法之過漢唐矣。太祖而下，如太宗之恭儉好文，真宗之寬仁慈愛，仁宗之力行恭儉，英宗之優禮大臣，庶幾其賢者歟？惜其仁厚有餘，而剛斷不足，此宋之治亦止於宋而已。夫法非自行，必本於道而後行；名非自立，必有其實而後立。古之人皆有以處乎此，而後世獲效之不古若，豈非以其或有體而無用，或有用而無體歟？
洪惟我朝太祖高皇帝創業垂統，用夏變夷，《大誥》申明五常之義，律令詳著萬法之條。養民有田，足國有賦，禦暴有兵，禁奸有刑。大綱畢正，萬目具舉，其弘模丕範，誠足以超越三王，垂示萬世矣。列聖相承，重光繼照。至於陛下，祖述憲章，克篤前烈。大孝尊親，上隆懽於慈極；彝倫敷叙，下疏愛於天潢。分田賦民，惟祖宗之成憲是遵；練兵用刑，惟祖宗之舊典是式。總萬善於一身，光百王於千載，其於道
translation_en:
…in our dynasty, when ministers commit offenses, punishment goes no further than removal from office: this is the rule of humane leniency. These eight practices indeed show that the ruling house’s traditions surpassed those of the Han and Tang. From Taizu onward, were not such rulers as Taizong, with his reverence, frugality, and love of learning; Zhenzong, with his leniency and kindness; Renzong, with his diligent practice of reverence and frugality; and Yingzong, with his generous courtesy toward high ministers, perhaps worthy sovereigns? Regrettably, they had more than enough benevolence and generosity but insufficient firmness and decisiveness. Thus the government of the Song attained only the level characteristic of the Song. Institutions cannot operate of themselves: they must be rooted in the Way before they can operate. A name cannot establish itself: it must have the corresponding substance before it can stand. The ancients all had means of handling these matters. That later generations achieved results inferior to those of antiquity—was this not because some possessed the underlying substance without its practical operation, while others possessed practical operation without the underlying substance?
We reverently reflect that Emperor Taizu Gao of our dynasty founded the realm and transmitted its succession, transforming the uncivilized through the civilization of Xia. His Grand Pronouncements (Da Gao) expounded the meaning of the Five Constant Virtues, while statutes and ordinances set forth in detail the provisions governing all affairs. There were fields to nourish the people, taxes to provide for the state, troops to repel violence, and punishments to restrain wrongdoing. Every major principle was properly established, and every detailed provision put into effect. His grand patterns and mighty examples truly sufficed to surpass the Three Kings and instruct ten thousand generations. Successive sage emperors inherited his work, their brilliance shining forth in turn. Now Your Majesty carries forward your forebears’ principles and follows their models, faithfully sustaining their glorious achievements. With supreme filial devotion you honor your parent, bringing joy above to your august mother; by duly ordering the constant human relationships, you extend affection below to the imperial clan. In allotting fields and taxing the people, you follow only the established institutions of your ancestors; in training troops and applying punishments, you take only their ancient precedents as your model. You unite all virtues in your own person and outshine the hundred kings across a thousand years. As for your understanding of the Way…

translation_en:
…the necessity of drawing upon both the Way and institutional models, and the principle that names and realities must sustain one another, are already clearly illuminated within Your Majesty’s profound mind. Yet you still wish to explore the subtle depths of the Way and examine in detail the establishment of institutions. As for names and realities, you wish to investigate why their mutual support brought good government under the Three Dynasties, and why, in later ages, their failure to support one another left government inferior to that of antiquity. Your servant believes that this depends on nothing other than a change within Your Majesty’s own mind. The human mind is supremely empty and supremely responsive: it is here that all principles are contained, and here that all affairs are met. Only when it is constrained by one’s endowment of vital energy and obscured by material desires do its entire substance and great functioning cease to be clear.

If Your Majesty can first bring clarity to your mind, restore its original rectitude, and remove the selfishness induced by external temptations, allowing neither the heterogeneous policies of later ages to impede you nor commonplace arguments for following established practice to sway and confuse you, then you will surely be able to explore the subtleties of the Way. As these find expression in daily life and the enduring human relationships, each will fully realize its proper and unchanging standard. As for institutional models, you will surely be able to examine their establishment in detail. As these take shape in the framework of government, laws, and regulations, all will contribute to the accomplishment of your lofty and far-reaching undertaking. When you investigate names and realities, you will recognize that the precision and thoroughness of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou were unlike the broad and cursory arrangements of the Han, Tang, and Song. How, then, could the distinction between their successes and failures require further argument to become clear?

Master Cheng said: “Only after possessing the spirit of ‘The Ospreys’ [Guan sui, apparently for Guan ju, ?] and ‘The Qilin’s Hooves’ [Lin zhi] can one implement the institutions and regulations of the Offices of Zhou.” From this we know that only by drawing upon both the Way and institutional models can we speak of good government. Confucius said: “When a gentleman gives something a name, it must be possible to express it in words.” From this we know that names and realities must sustain one another before they can be transmitted into the distant future. Thus, who could say that drawing upon both the Way and institutional models, and making names and realities sustain one another, does not lie within Your Majesty’s own mind? Nevertheless, although a ruler’s government is indeed rooted in his mind, the essential means of rectifying that mind…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
尤在於意誠大學曰欲正其心者先誠其意使意有
不誠則無以正其心而推於治矣臣願
陛下窮理以致其知存誠以立其本而凡一念將發之頃
必察其天理人欲之幾天理邪必循之而造其極人
欲邪必遏之而絕其根
大庭廣衆之中固此誠也深宫燕閒之地亦此誠也念
念相承無少間斷則一理渾融
萬幾密勿將見體用兼全本末具舉
陛下今日之治道與三王同一道心之精微
陛下今日之治法與三王同一時中之妙用而盛治之效
===
亦將與三代竝隆矣區區漢唐宋之治何足言哉昔
宋儒朱熹入對有戒其勿以正心誠意之說進者熹
曰吾平生所學在此四字豈敢隱黙以欺吾君臣嘗
誦此以自箴警今承
明詔故於篇終直舉平昔所得於學者以為獻亦何敢
負所學以欺吾
君父邪臣不勝惓惓之至伏惟
陛下留神察焉則天下幸甚萬世幸甚臣謹對

陛下留神察焉則天下幸甚萬世幸甚臣謹對
punctuated:
尤在於意誠。《大學》曰：「欲正其心者，先誠其意。」使意有不誠，則無以正其心而推於治矣。臣願陛下窮理以致其知，存誠以立其本，而凡一念將發之頃，必察其天理人欲之幾。天理邪？必循之而造其極；人欲邪？必遏之而絕其根。大庭廣衆之中固此誠也，深宫燕閒之地亦此誠也。念念相承，無少間斷，則一理渾融，萬幾密勿。將見體用兼全，本末具舉，陛下今日之治道，與三王同一道心之精微；陛下今日之治法，與三王同一時中之妙用，而盛治之效亦將與三代竝隆矣。區區漢唐宋之治，何足言哉！

昔宋儒朱熹入對，有戒其勿以正心誠意之說進者。熹曰：「吾平生所學在此四字，豈敢隱黙以欺吾君？」臣嘗誦此以自箴警。今承明詔，故於篇終直舉平昔所得於學者以為獻，亦何敢負所學以欺吾君父邪？臣不勝惓惓之至，伏惟陛下留神察焉，則天下幸甚，萬世幸甚。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…lies especially in making the intentions sincere. The Great Learning says: “Those who wish to rectify their minds first make their intentions sincere.” If the intentions lack sincerity, there is no means of rectifying the mind and extending this to government. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would investigate principle to extend your knowledge and preserve sincerity to establish your foundation. Whenever a thought is about to arise, you must examine its incipient tendency toward heavenly principle or human desire. Is it heavenly principle? Then follow it to its fullest realization. Is it human desire? Then restrain it and sever its root. Amid the assembled multitude in the great court, maintain this sincerity; in the leisure and seclusion of the inner palace, maintain this same sincerity. If thought succeeds thought without the slightest interruption, the one principle will be wholly integrated, and the myriad affairs of state attended to with diligence. Then substance and function will both be complete, and root and branches alike attended to. Your Majesty’s Way of governing today will share with the Three Kings the same subtlety of the moral mind; Your Majesty’s methods of governing today will share with the Three Kings the same wondrous application of acting in accordance with the mean as circumstances require. The achievements of flourishing government will likewise rival the grandeur of the Three Dynasties. How could the paltry government of the Han, Tang, and Song merit mention!

Formerly, when the Song scholar Zhu Xi was about to address the throne, someone warned him not to present the teaching of rectifying the mind and making the intentions sincere. Zhu Xi said: “What I have studied throughout my life lies in these four characters. How could I dare conceal it in silence and thereby deceive my ruler?” Your servant has often recited this to admonish and caution himself. Now, having received your enlightened edict, I therefore conclude this essay by directly presenting what I have gained from my customary studies. How could I dare betray what I have learned and thereby deceive my ruler and father? Your servant’s earnest devotion knows no bounds. I humbly ask that Your Majesty give this your attentive consideration. Then all under Heaven would be most fortunate, and all generations to come would be most fortunate. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
黃珣
臣對臣聞治本於道而道之行寓於法道本於心而
心之主在乎誠蓋道為出治之本法乃輔治之具而
其立法必有名以表之有實以稱之是皆可相有而
不可相無者也苟非本於一心之誠則猶無源之水
雖盈而易涸無本之木雖植而必僵何以使道法之
兼舉名實之相須而成極至之治哉惟古三代之君
能存此心之誠故行道則為至道立法則為良法名
當其實實稱其名此夏之所以為夏商之所以為商
周之所以為周也下逮漢唐宋諸君非不欲致其治
===
也但不能存其心耳非不欲存其心也但不能主於
誠耳故或大綱正而萬目不舉或萬目舉而大綱不
正名無以當其實實無以稱其名此漢之所以止於漢
唐所以止於唐宋所以止於宋也欽惟
皇帝陛下
聰明睿知
孝友温恭一德清明萬境澄澈行
祖宗列聖之道以制治一此心之誠不雜也守
祖宗列聖之法以保邦一此心之誠不渝也大綱畢正萬
目具舉名當其實實稱其名所以躋世雍熙追蹤三

punctuated:
黃珣

臣對：臣聞治本於道，而道之行寓於法；道本於心，而心之主在乎誠。蓋道為出治之本，法乃輔治之具，而其立法，必有名以表之，有實以稱之，是皆可相有而不可相無者也。苟非本於一心之誠，則猶無源之水，雖盈而易涸；無本之木，雖植而必僵。何以使道法之兼舉、名實之相須，而成極至之治哉？惟古三代之君能存此心之誠，故行道則為至道，立法則為良法，名當其實，實稱其名，此夏之所以為夏、商之所以為商、周之所以為周也。下逮漢唐宋諸君，非不欲致其治也，但不能存其心耳；非不欲存其心也，但不能主於誠耳。故或大綱正而萬目不舉，或萬目舉而大綱不正，名無以當其實，實無以稱其名，此漢之所以止於漢、唐所以止於唐、宋所以止於宋也。

欽惟皇帝陛下，聰明睿知，孝友温恭，一德清明，萬境澄澈。行祖宗列聖之道以制治，一此心之誠不雜也；守祖宗列聖之法以保邦，一此心之誠不渝也。大綱畢正，萬目具舉，名當其實，實稱其名，所以躋世雍熙、追蹤三
translation_en:
Huang Xun

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that governance is rooted in the Way, while the practice of the Way resides in laws; the Way is rooted in the heart, while what governs the heart is sincerity. The Way is the foundation from which good governance proceeds, and laws are instruments that assist it. When laws are established, there must be names to express them and substance to correspond to those names. These must coexist; none can do without the others. Unless they are rooted in the sincerity of a single heart, they are like water without a source, which, though full, readily dries up, or a tree without roots, which, though planted, will surely fall. How, then, could the Way and laws both be put into effect, and names and substance sustain one another, to achieve governance of the utmost perfection? Only the rulers of the ancient Three Dynasties could preserve this sincerity of heart. Thus, the Way they practiced was the highest Way, and the laws they established were good laws. Names matched their substance, and substance corresponded to its names. This is what made Xia Xia, Shang Shang, and Zhou Zhou. Coming down to the rulers of Han, Tang, and Song, it was not that they did not wish to achieve such governance, but that they could not preserve their hearts. It was not that they did not wish to preserve their hearts, but that they could not make sincerity their guiding principle. Consequently, either the main framework was correct but its myriad particulars were not put into effect, or the myriad particulars were put into effect but the main framework was not correct. Names could not match their substance, and substance could not correspond to its names. This is why Han remained merely Han, Tang merely Tang, and Song merely Song.

I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor is perceptive, enlightened, discerning, and wise; filial, devoted to your brothers, gentle, and reverent. Your undivided virtue is pure and bright, and all within your purview is limpid and clear. You practice the Way of your sagely imperial forebears to establish good governance, keeping the sincerity of this heart undivided and unmixed. You uphold the laws of your sagely imperial forebears to safeguard the realm, keeping the sincerity of this heart undivided and unchanging. The main framework is entirely correct, and all its myriad particulars are put into effect. Names match their substance, and substance corresponds to its names. The means by which you raise the age to harmony and prosperity and follow in the footsteps of the Three…

貽子孫制官刑以儆有位六典八法之皆全五禮六
樂之咸備法亦無不舉焉道無不正法無不舉非無
自也一本於此心之誠也
聖策諭以三代之治有紀綱法度而疑在道不在法臣愚
有以知
陛下欲行治道舉治法以成至治即孔子〔所謂道之以致〕
punctuated:
代也，在於此矣。然而圖治之心，惟日不足，迺於萬幾之餘，進臣等于廷陛之下，諄諄懇切，訪以治道，必欲求一定之論，以追復三代之盛。臣雖至愚，敢不拜手稽首，殫厥心思，以對揚休命於萬一乎？臣竊惟古之為治，有道焉，有法焉。道者，大綱也；法者，萬目也。法非道無所本，道非法無所寓。故必道與法兼舉，然後可以言乎治而無失。法之所立，有名焉，有實焉。名者，實之賓也；實者，名之主也。名非實無以顯，實非名不能永。故必名與實相須，然後可以傳諸遠而無弊。
臣甞觀於三代之治，大禹率由典常而文命四敷，成湯肇脩人紀而九圍是式，文王兹迪彞教，武王重民五教，道固無不正也。底慎財賦而設學校之教，軍將皆卿而立司馬之政，有典則以貽子孫，制官刑以儆有位，六典八法之皆全，五禮六樂之咸備，法亦無不舉焉。道無不正，法無不舉，非無自也，一本於此心之誠也。
聖策詢以三代之治有紀綱法度，而疑在道不在法。臣愚有以知陛下欲行治道、舉治法，以成至治，即孔子所謂「道之以政」
translation_en:
…the Three Dynasties: herein lies the means of achieving this. Yet Your Majesty’s desire for good government finds each day insufficient. Amid your myriad duties, you have summoned us, your servants, before the palace steps and earnestly and sincerely questioned us about the Way of governing, determined to obtain a settled judgment by which to recover the flourishing rule of the Three Dynasties. Though your servant is utterly ignorant, how could I fail to bow with clasped hands, knock my head to the ground, and exhaust my thoughts in answering and honoring even a ten-thousandth part of your gracious command? Your servant humbly considers that ancient government possessed both a Way and institutions. The Way is the overarching framework; institutions are its myriad particulars. Without the Way, institutions have no foundation; without institutions, the Way has no embodiment. Only when both the Way and institutions are put into effect can one speak of government without failings. What institutions establish has both names and realities. Names are the guests of realities; realities are the hosts of names. Without realities, names have no means of becoming manifest; without names, realities cannot endure. Only when names and realities sustain one another can they be transmitted into the distant future without harm.
Your servant has examined the government of the Three Dynasties. Yu the Great followed the established norms, and his civilizing influence spread throughout the four quarters. Cheng Tang first put human relationships in order, and the nine regions took him as their model. King Wen guided people through the constant teachings; King Wu placed weight on the five teachings governing human relationships. Their Way was thus correct in every respect. They exercised utmost care over revenues and taxation and established instruction in schools; their army commanders were all ministers, and they established the administration of the Minister of War. They had statutes and standards to bequeath to their descendants and instituted punishments for officials to admonish those holding office. The six administrative codes and eight administrative regulations were complete; the five rites and six musical traditions were all provided for. Their institutions, too, were fully implemented. That their Way was correct in every respect and their institutions fully implemented was not without a source: all was rooted in the sincerity of this heart.
Your Majesty’s policy question asks about the guiding principles and institutional standards of government under the Three Dynasties, while raising the question whether good government lay in the Way rather than in institutions. Your ignorant servant can thereby discern Your Majesty’s desire to practice the Way of governing and implement its institutions in order to achieve consummate government. This is precisely what Confucius meant by “Guide them through administrative measures…”

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
齊之以刑道之以德齊之以禮之意也彼謂在道不
在法者非不用法也但不專於法耳不然則繼以仁
政之說不幾於戾乎三代之法其建學以教民也如
庠以養老為義序以習射為義庠序之名立而家無
不學之人人必行藝之著制產以養民也如鄉遂用
貢法都鄙用助法貢助之名立而野無不耕之土下
無游惰之民以兵言之簡其車賦歷其卒伍不徒立
軍旅什伍之名而已而干城敵愾之人自滿於戎行
以刑言之凡制五刑必即天倫不徒立墨劓剕宮之
名而已而枉撓不當之弊何有於官府名以永其實
===
實以稱其名非無故也一本於此心之誠也
聖策詢以聖王立法必有名以表實而疑貴實不貴名臣
愚有以知
陛下欲求夫實稱其名以立良法即孔子所謂名之必可
言言之必可行之意也彼謂貴實不貴名者非不貴
名也但不務其名耳不然則必也正名之說不幾於
迂乎臣又觀於漢唐宋之時漢高祖發義帝之喪正
丁公之罪而君臣之義明禮太公之尊悟四皓之至
而父□之倫厚睦周親也連城以封同姓崇聖道也
太牢以祀孔子大綱之正可美也嗣是而治者若文

名而已而枉撓不當之弊何有於官府名以求其實
實以稱其名非無故也一本於此心之誠也
===
聖策詢以聖王立法必有名以表實而疑貴實不貴名臣
愚有以知
陛下欲求夫實稱其名以立良法即孔子所謂名之必可
言言之必可行之意也彼謂貴實不貴名者非不貴
名也但不務其名耳不然則必也正名之說不幾於
迂乎臣又觀於漢唐宋之時漢高祖發義帝之喪正
丁公之罪而君臣之義明禮太公之尊悟四皓之至
而父子之倫厚睦周親也連城以封同姓崇聖道也
太牢以祀孔子大綱之正可羨也嗣是而治者若文
punctuated:
齊之以刑，道之以德，齊之以禮之意也。彼謂在道不在法者，非不用法也，但不專於法耳。不然，則繼以仁政之說，不幾於戾乎？三代之法，其建學以教民也，如庠以養老為義，序以習射為義。庠序之名立，而家無不學之人，人必行藝之著。制產以養民也，如鄉遂用貢法，都鄙用助法。貢助之名立，而野無不耕之土，下無游惰之民。以兵言之，簡其車賦，歷其卒伍，不徒立軍旅什伍之名而已，而干城敵愾之人自滿於戎行。以刑言之，凡制五刑，必即天倫，不徒立墨劓剕宮之名而已，而枉撓不當之弊，何有於官府？名以永其實，實以稱其名，非無故也，一本於此心之誠也。
聖策詢以聖王立法必有名以表實，而疑貴實不貴名。臣愚有以知陛下欲求夫實稱其名，以立良法，即孔子所謂名之必可言，言之必可行之意也。彼謂貴實不貴名者，非不貴名也，但不務其名耳。不然，則必也正名之說，不幾於迂乎？臣又觀於漢唐宋之時，漢高祖發義帝之喪，正丁公之罪，而君臣之義明；禮太公之尊，悟四皓之至，而父□之倫厚。睦周親也，連城以封同姓；崇聖道也，太牢以祀孔子。大綱之正，可美也。嗣是而治者，若文
translation_en:
…“keep them in order through punishments; guide them through virtue and keep them in order through ritual”—this is the meaning. Those who say that government rests on the Way rather than on laws do not mean that laws should not be used, but merely that one should not rely exclusively upon them. Otherwise, would the ensuing discussion of benevolent government not verge on contradiction? Under the laws of the Three Dynasties, schools were established to teach the people: the xiang took its meaning from providing for the aged, and the xu from practicing archery. Once the institutions bearing these names were established, no household lacked someone who studied, and everyone distinguished himself in conduct and accomplishments. In establishing livelihoods to sustain the people, the gong system of tribute was used in the rural districts and outer districts, and the zhu system of labor assistance in the domains and outlying settlements. Once these systems bearing the names gong and zhu were established, no land in the countryside went untilled, and no one among the common people remained idle. As for military affairs, they inspected the chariot levies and reviewed the ranks of soldiers. They did not merely establish the names of armies, brigades, and units of ten and five: the ranks naturally filled with men who served as shields and walls and confronted the enemy with righteous anger. As for punishments, whenever they instituted the Five Punishments, they necessarily conformed to the relationships ordained by Heaven. They did not merely establish the names of tattooing, cutting off the nose, amputating the feet, and castration. How, then, could abuses involving perversion, distortion, or improper application of the law arise in government offices? Names perpetuated their substance, and substance matched its names. This was not without a cause: it was rooted entirely in the sincerity of this mind.
Your Majesty’s policy question asks about the sage kings’ establishment of laws, which necessarily had names to express their substance, and raises a doubt about valuing substance rather than names. Your foolish servant thus understands that Your Majesty wishes to ensure that substance matches its name, so as to establish good laws. This is precisely what Confucius meant when he said that names must permit things to be spoken of, and what is spoken must permit things to be carried out. Those who say that substance should be valued rather than names do not mean that names are without value, but merely that one should not pursue names alone. Otherwise, would the statement that one must rectify names not verge on impracticality? Your servant has also examined the times of the Han, Tang, and Song. Emperor Gaozu of Han proclaimed mourning for Emperor Yi and duly punished Ding Gong’s crime, thereby making clear the righteous relationship between ruler and minister. He honored the exalted status of Taigong and grasped the significance of the arrival of the Four Hoary Elders, thereby strengthening the relationship between father and □ [?]. To maintain harmony among his closest kin, he enfeoffed men of his own surname with adjoining cities; to honor the Way of the sages, he offered the full complement of sacrificial animals to Confucius. The correctness of his principal ordering of government deserves admiration. Among those who subsequently ruled were such men as Wen…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
帝之以德化民武帝之雄才大畧宣帝之勵精圖治
光武之克復舊物明帝之宅心恭儉章帝之務從寬
厚皆漢之賢君固宜有七制之稱也自七制之中而
論之則尊師重傅臨雍拜老者豈不為知重道而優
乎惜夫耳目為明流於苛察尚乏弘人之度優者如
此餘可知矣傳曰徒善不足以為政漢大綱雖正萬
目未舉所謂徒善也則漢之治不能繼美於周也明
矣原其所自豈非此心之誠未至而雜於霸歟
聖策以漢大綱正而治不能繼美周及以七制之優者為
問臣愚有以知
===
陛下欲鑒漢之失而思匹休於三代容肯徒善而已哉唐
太宗之制田賦也易粟米之征而為租易布縷之征
而為調易力役之征而為庸故有田則有租有家則
有調有身則有庸蓋依稀乎先王田賦之制其制兵
刑也分百人千人萬人之伍而有下府中府上府之
名去斷趾鞭背之刑而有三覆五覆之奏蓋彷彿乎
先王兵刑之制萬目之舉可嘉也嗣是而治者若玄
宗勵精政事好賢樂善開元之間幾致太平憲宗剛
明果斷志平僭叛能用忠謀不惑群議皆唐之賢君
固宜有三宗之稱也自三宗之內而論之則祖宗威

光武之克復舊物明帝之食心恭儉章帝之務從寬

乎惜夫耳目為明流於苛察尚之弘人之度優著如
此餘可知矣傳曰徒善不足以為政漢大綱雖正爲
目未舉所謂徒善也則漢之治不能繼美於周也明
矣原其所自豈非此心之誠未至而雜於霸歟
聖策以漢大綱正而治不能繼于成周及以七制之優者為
問臣愚有以知
===
陛下欲鑒漢之失而思匹休於三代容肯徒善而已哉唐
太宗之制田賦也易粟帛之征而為租易布縷之征
而為調易力役之征而為庸故有田則有租有家則
有調有身則有庸蓋依稀乎先王田賦之制其制兵
刑也分百人千人萬人之伍而有下府中府上府之
名去斷趾鞭背之刑而有三覆五覆之奏蓋彷彿乎
先王兵刑之制萬目之舉可嘉也嗣是而治者君玄
宗勵精政事好賢樂善開元之間幾致太平憲宗剛
明果斷志平僭叛能用忠謀不惑群議皆唐之賢君
固宜有三宗之稱也自三宗之內而論之則祖宗威
punctuated:
帝之以德化民，武帝之雄才大畧，宣帝之勵精圖治，光武之克復舊物，明帝之宅心恭儉，章帝之務從寬厚，皆漢之賢君，固宜有七制之稱也。自七制之中而論之，則尊師重傅、臨雍拜老者，豈不為知重道而優乎？惜夫耳目為明，流於苛察，尚乏弘人之度。優者如此，餘可知矣。傳曰：「徒善不足以為政。」漢大綱雖正，萬目未舉，所謂徒善也。則漢之治不能繼美於周也，明矣。原其所自，豈非此心之誠未至而雜於霸歟？
聖策以漢大綱正而治不能繼美周，及以七制之優者為問。臣愚有以知陛下欲鑒漢之失，而思匹休於三代，容肯徒善而已哉？唐太宗之制田賦也，易粟米之征而為租，易布縷之征而為調，易力役之征而為庸。故有田則有租，有家則有調，有身則有庸，蓋依稀乎先王田賦之制。其制兵刑也，分百人、千人、萬人之伍，而有下府、中府、上府之名；去斷趾鞭背之刑，而有三覆、五覆之奏，蓋彷彿乎先王兵刑之制。萬目之舉，可嘉也。嗣是而治者，若玄宗勵精政事，好賢樂善，開元之間幾致太平；憲宗剛明果斷，志平僭叛，能用忠謀，不惑群議，皆唐之賢君，固宜有三宗之稱也。自三宗之內而論之，則祖宗威
translation_en:
…Emperor Wen transformed the people through virtue; Emperor Wu possessed outstanding talent and broad strategic vision; Emperor Xuan devoted himself energetically to good government; Guangwu recovered the former imperial inheritance; Emperor Ming set his heart on reverence and frugality; and Emperor Zhang strove to be generous and forbearing. All were worthy rulers of the Han, and deserved the collective designation “the Seven Reigns.” Among these seven, was not the one who honored teachers and tutors, visited the imperial academy, and bowed to the elders superior in understanding the importance of the Way? Regrettably, he took what his ears and eyes perceived as true discernment and descended into harsh scrutiny, still lacking the magnanimity to accommodate others. If even the superior ruler was like this, one can infer what the others were like. The commentary says: “Good intentions alone are insufficient for government.” Although the Han set the main guiding principles right, it did not put all the detailed measures into effect. This is what is meant by “good intentions alone.” Clearly, then, Han government could not carry forward the excellence of the Zhou. If we trace this to its source, was it not because the sincerity of the ruler’s heart was incomplete and mixed with the pursuit of hegemony?
Your Majesty’s policy question asks why, although the Han’s main guiding principles were correct, its government could not continue the excellence of the Zhou, and which of the Seven Reigns was superior. Foolish though I am, I understand from this that Your Majesty wishes to take warning from the Han’s failings and rival the glory of the Three Dynasties. How could you be content with good intentions alone? When Taizong of the Tang established the land-tax system, he changed the levy on grain into the grain tax (zu), the levy on cloth and thread into the textile tax (diao), and the levy of labor service into the labor-service commutation (yong). Thus, possession of land entailed the grain tax, having a household entailed the textile tax, and being an individual entailed the labor-service commutation. This bore some resemblance to the land-tax system of the ancient kings. In organizing military affairs and punishments, he divided the troops into units of a hundred, a thousand, and ten thousand, with commands designated lower, middle, and upper [?]. He abolished the punishments of cutting off toes and flogging the back, and instituted memorials requesting three or five reviews of capital sentences. This approximated the ancient kings’ arrangements for military affairs and punishments. Putting these detailed measures into effect was commendable. Among those who subsequently ruled, Xuanzong applied himself diligently to government, esteemed worthy men, and delighted in goodness, nearly bringing about perfect peace during the Kaiyuan era. Xianzong was resolute, discerning, and decisive, determined to suppress usurpers and rebels; he could employ loyal counsel without being swayed by competing opinions. Both were worthy Tang rulers, and the three rightly merited the collective designation “the Three Zong.” Among these three, then, the ancestors’ authority…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
令既□撰者豈不為能守法而賢乎惜夫信用非
人□烈其業卒罹不測之禍賢者如此餘可見矣傳
曰徒善不能以自行唐萬目雖舉大綱不正所謂徒
法也則唐之治不能相遠於漢也宜矣跡其所由豈
非此心之誠未至而雜於夷歟
聖策以唐萬目舉而治不相遠於漢及以三宗之賢者為
問臣愚有以知
陛下欲鑒唐之失而思媲美於三代容肯徒法而已哉至
如宋太祖興仁義之治知九經之義母事周后子愛
少帝待降主以賓禮易節鎮以儒臣金匱一盟而允
===
盡母子兄弟之道杯酒一言而克全君臣勳戚之義
大綱固正矣然以詩賦記誦而取士以科名資歷而
叙位選宿衛而沿五代之舊教宗室而失先王之制
萬目則未能盡舉焉宋之大綱正萬目未盡舉疑若
不及於唐矣然而其家法之善則有非漢唐之所可
及者觀其事母后皆朝夕見此事親之法也事大長
公主以姑禮此事長之法也宮禁極其嚴密則治內
之法以得外戚皆不預政則待外戚之法以得他如
尚儉□法無一不踐其實尚禮寬仁之法無一
不得□當此又家法之善超越漢唐而足以致太平

punctuated:
令既□撰者，豈不為能守法而賢乎？惜夫信用非人，□烈其業，卒罹不測之禍。賢者如此，餘可見矣。傳曰：「徒善不能以自行。」唐萬目雖舉，大綱不正，所謂徒法也。則唐之治不能相遠於漢也，宜矣。跡其所由，豈非此心之誠未至而雜於夷歟？
聖策以唐萬目舉而治不相遠於漢，及以三宗之賢者為問。臣愚有以知陛下欲鑒唐之失，而思媲美於三代，容肯徒法而已哉？至如宋太祖興仁義之治，知九經之義，母事周后，子愛少帝，待降主以賓禮，易節鎮以儒臣，金匱一盟而允盡母子兄弟之道，杯酒一言而克全君臣勳戚之義，大綱固正矣。然以詩賦記誦而取士，以科名資歷而叙位，選宿衛而沿五代之舊，教宗室而失先王之制，萬目則未能盡舉焉。宋之大綱正，萬目未盡舉，疑若不及於唐矣。然而其家法之善，則有非漢唐之所可及者。觀其事母后，皆朝夕見，此事親之法也；事大長公主以姑禮，此事長之法也。宮禁極其嚴密，則治內之法以得；外戚皆不預政，則待外戚之法以得。他如尚儉□法，無一不踐其實；尚禮寬仁之法，無一不得□當。此又家法之善，超越漢唐，而足以致太平
translation_en:
…the commands having already □ [?]—could those who maintained them not be considered worthy for their ability to uphold established institutions? Regrettably, they trusted and employed the wrong men, □ their achievements [?], and ultimately suffered unforeseen calamities. If even the worthy were like this, the others may readily be judged. The commentary says: “Goodness alone cannot put itself into practice” [?]. Although the Tang attended to the myriad particulars, its overarching principles were not correct: this is what is meant by mere institutions. It is therefore only fitting that Tang governance could not greatly surpass that of the Han. Tracing the cause, was it not that the sincerity of their hearts fell short and was mixed with barbarian ways?
Your Majesty’s sagely policy question asks why, although the Tang attended to the myriad particulars, its governance did not greatly surpass that of the Han, and asks also about the worthiness of the three eminent Tang emperors. Your foolish servant thus understands that Your Majesty wishes to take warning from the Tang’s failings and hopes to match the excellence of the Three Dynasties. How could you be willing to rest content with mere institutions?
As for Taizu of the Song, he established governance through benevolence and righteousness and understood the meaning of the nine guiding principles. He served the Zhou empress as a mother and loved the young emperor as a son. He treated surrendered rulers with the courtesy due to guests and replaced regional military commanders with Confucian officials. Through the single oath preserved in the golden coffer, he truly fulfilled the proper relations between mother and son and between brothers; through a word over a cup of wine, he fully preserved the obligations between ruler and ministers and toward meritorious servants and imperial relatives. His overarching principles were indeed correct. Yet he selected officials through poetry, rhapsodies, memorization, and recitation, and assigned rank according to examination standing and seniority. In selecting palace guards, he followed the old practices of the Five Dynasties; in educating the imperial clan, he departed from the institutions of the ancient kings. Thus he could not attend fully to the myriad particulars.
The Song’s overarching principles were correct, but its myriad particulars were not all attended to, so it might seem inferior to the Tang. Yet the excellence of its dynastic household rules included things beyond the reach of either Han or Tang. Consider how its emperors attended upon their empress mothers, seeing them morning and evening: this was their rule for serving parents. They served the Senior Princess Imperial with the courtesy due to a paternal aunt: this was their rule for serving elders. The palace prohibitions were exceedingly strict, so their rules for governing the inner palace were properly established [?]. Imperial relatives by marriage took no part in government, so their rules for treating those relatives were properly established [?]. As for other rules, such as those honoring frugality □ [?], there was not one whose substance they failed to put into practice; among the rules honoring ritual propriety, generosity, and benevolence, there was not one that failed to attain □ propriety [?]. Here again, the excellence of their dynastic household rules surpassed that of Han and Tang and was sufficient to bring about great peace…

之就其君而論之若太宗之豐功偉績史不絶
書□□之政從簡易寬仁慈愛皆可謂有宋守成之
賢君又不若仁宗之恭儉仁恕擢任賢才上以體一
祖二宗之心下以肇濂洛道統之源存心制治無可
議者為尤賢也然郭后之事白璧微瑕是宋之治不
能比隆於三代者又豈非此心之誠未至而不能無
所雜歟
聖策及此臣愚又有以知
陛下是心欲鑒有宋之失而必復三代之治也天下臣民
何其幸哉仰惟
===
陛下望道未見求言若渴又於
聖策終篇欲聞道法名實之詳為當今取舍之宜是在
聖心一轉移之間有餘裕矣而乃下詢微陋臣愚以為道
也者日用事物當然之理也原於天命具於人心其
文則易書詩禮樂春秋其倫則君臣父子夫婦長幼
朋友於此而探之則精微之蘊豈外是邪法也者古
昔帝王致治之具也防範人心綱維世教所以勸善
而懲惡者在是所以利用而厚生者在是於此而參
之則制作之詳不在是邪三代之治道法兼舉名實
相□□底雍熈而非後世之所能及也漢唐宋

punctuated:
之。就其君而論之，若太宗之豐功偉績，史不絶書，□□之政，從簡易，寬仁慈愛，皆可謂有宋守成之賢君。又不若仁宗之恭儉仁恕，擢任賢才，上以體一祖二宗之心，下以肇濂洛道統之源，存心制治，無可議者，為尤賢也。然郭后之事，白璧微瑕，是宋之治不能比隆於三代者，又豈非此心之誠未至而不能無所雜歟？聖策及此，臣愚又有以知陛下是心欲鑒有宋之失，而必復三代之治也。天下臣民何其幸哉！
仰惟陛下望道未見，求言若渴，又於聖策終篇欲聞道法名實之詳，為當今取舍之宜，是在聖心一轉移之間有餘裕矣，而乃下詢微陋。臣愚以為，道也者，日用事物當然之理也，原於天命，具於人心。其文則《易》《書》《詩》《禮》《樂》《春秋》，其倫則君臣、父子、夫婦、長幼、朋友。於此而探之，則精微之蘊豈外是邪？法也者，古昔帝王致治之具也，防範人心，綱維世教。所以勸善而懲惡者在是，所以利用而厚生者在是。於此而參之，則制作之詳不在是邪？三代之治，道法兼舉，名實相□□底雍熈，而非後世之所能及也。漢唐宋
translation_en:
… Turning to its rulers, Taizong’s great achievements and mighty deeds are recorded throughout the histories; the government of □□ [?] followed simplicity and ease and displayed magnanimity, benevolence, kindness, and love. These may all be called worthy Song rulers who preserved the inherited achievement. Yet they did not equal Renzong, whose reverence, frugality, benevolence, and forbearance, and whose promotion and employment of worthy talent, embodied the intentions of the founding ancestor and the two ancestral emperors before him and opened the source of the transmission of the Way at Lian and Luo for those who followed. In cultivating his intentions and ordering government, he was beyond reproach and was thus especially worthy. Nevertheless, the affair of Empress Guo was a slight flaw in white jade. That Song government could not equal the flourishing rule of the Three Dynasties—was this not also because the sincerity of this heart had not reached perfection and could not remain free of admixture? Your Majesty’s policy question touches upon this, allowing your foolish servant further to perceive that Your Majesty’s heart desires to take warning from the Song’s failings and resolutely restore the government of the Three Dynasties. How fortunate are all the subjects and people of the realm!
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty looks toward the Way as though you had not yet seen it and seeks counsel as one thirsting for water. At the close of your imperial policy question, you further wish to hear a detailed account of the Way and institutions, names and realities, so as to determine what should appropriately be adopted or rejected today. A single shift in your sagely heart would more than suffice for this, yet you stoop to consult one so humble and ignorant. Your foolish servant considers the Way to be the principles of what ought to be in everyday affairs and things. It originates in Heaven’s mandate and is inherent in the human heart. Its textual expressions are the Changes, Documents, Odes, Rites, Music, and Spring and Autumn Annals; its human relationships are those between ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, and friends. If one searches within these, could its subtle and profound riches lie anywhere outside them? Institutions are the instruments by which the emperors and kings of antiquity brought about good government. They restrain the human heart and uphold moral teaching in the world. Herein lie the means of encouraging good and punishing evil, and herein lie the means of making resources useful and enriching the people’s livelihood. If one examines these, are not the details of institutional arrangements to be found here? Under the government of the Three Dynasties, the Way and institutions were both put into practice; names and realities mutually … [?], bringing about harmony and prosperity beyond what later ages could attain. The Han, Tang, and Song …

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
廢名實相違所以治不古若而不能久
也夫既知三代之治如此漢唐宋之治如
彼則取舎其有不明也哉舎彼而不行取此而必行
則治道其有不成也哉雖然勤始怠終乃古今之通
弊進銳退速實天下之同情臣所陳精微之蘊
陛下固已深究之然道至廣而無窮願
陛下以此心之誠始終體而行之務有以得其實則如孔
子所謂聖人久於其道而天下化成矣臣所陳制作
之詳
陛下固已身行之然法有時而或弊願
===
陛下以此心之誠始終守而行之務有以臻其實則如張
子所謂法立而能守則德可久業可大矣三代名實
相須之迹漢唐宋不相須之弊臣悉陳之矣然知之
非艱行之惟艱願
陛下推此心之誠而求之以今日之已行求他日所未行
必循名以責實使名實相須者再見於
盛世以今日之不為鑒他日所忍為不失實以務名使
名實相違者不形於政治則如程子所謂至誠一心
以□□之治為必可行不狃滯於近規必期致天下
如三代之世矣若此則

punctuated: 廢，名實相違，所以治不古若而不能久也。夫既知三代之治如此，漢唐宋之治如彼，則取舎其有不明也哉？舎彼而不行，取此而必行，則治道其有不成也哉？雖然，勤始怠終，乃古今之通弊；進銳退速，實天下之同情。臣所陳精微之蘊，陛下固已深究之，然道至廣而無窮，願陛下以此心之誠，始終體而行之，務有以得其實，則如孔子所謂「聖人久於其道而天下化成矣」。臣所陳制作之詳，陛下固已身行之，然法有時而或弊，願陛下以此心之誠，始終守而行之，務有以臻其實，則如張子所謂「法立而能守，則德可久，業可大矣」。三代名實相須之迹，漢唐宋不相須之弊，臣悉陳之矣。然知之非艱，行之惟艱，願陛下推此心之誠而求之，以今日之已行，求他日所未行，必循名以責實，使名實相須者再見於盛世；以今日之不為，鑒他日所忍為，不失實以務名，使名實相違者不形於政治，則如程子所謂「至誠一心，以□□之治為必可行，不狃滯於近規，必期致天下如三代之世矣」。若此，則
translation_en: …were abandoned, and names and realities diverged. Thus government did not equal that of antiquity and could not endure. Once we know that the Three Dynasties governed in this way, and the Han, Tang, and Song in that way, can there be any uncertainty about what to adopt and what to reject? If we reject the latter and do not practice it, adopt the former and unfailingly put it into practice, how could the way of good government fail to be realized? Nevertheless, diligence at the outset and negligence at the end are a common failing, ancient and modern; advancing eagerly and retreating swiftly are tendencies shared by all under Heaven. Your Majesty has already investigated deeply the subtle principles that your servant has set forth. Yet the Way is exceedingly broad and inexhaustible. I ask Your Majesty, with the sincerity of this heart, to embody and practice it from beginning to end, striving to grasp its substance. Then it will be as Kongzi said: “The sage perseveres in his Way, and the transformation of all under Heaven is accomplished.” Your Majesty has already personally put into practice the detailed institutions that your servant has set forth. Yet institutions may at times develop defects. I ask Your Majesty, with the sincerity of this heart, to uphold and practice them from beginning to end, striving to realize their substance. Then it will be as Master Zhang said: “Once institutions are established, if they can be upheld, virtue can endure and achievement can become great.” Your servant has fully set forth the evidence of how names and realities sustained one another under the Three Dynasties, and the failings that arose when they did not sustain one another under the Han, Tang, and Song. Yet knowing is not difficult; putting knowledge into practice is difficult. I ask Your Majesty to extend the sincerity of this heart in pursuing this: take what has already been practiced today as the basis for seeking what remains to be practiced in days to come. Always demand the reality corresponding to the name, so that the mutual support of names and realities may appear again in this flourishing age. Take what you refrain from doing today as a warning against what you might bring yourself to do in days to come. Do not sacrifice substance in pursuit of reputation, so that divergence between names and realities may not appear in government. Then it will be as Master Cheng said: “With utmost sincerity and an undivided heart, regard the government of □□ [?] as certainly practicable; do not become confined by habitual adherence to recent precedents, but resolve to bring all under Heaven to a condition like that of the Three Dynasties.” If this is so, then…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
之所□□者必合乎天理所舍者必適□時宜天下之
大□□而益正天下之萬目於此而益舉由是可
以格天心而正人極由是可以貞百度而一民心由
是可以綿
宗社於萬萬年之遠而三代雍熈之盛端在
今日矣彼區區漢唐宋之治奚足言哉夫克臻治效之
盛一本於此心之誠如此臣故始終以此心之誠為
陛下獻者此愚臣遇得言之時盡獻言之誠以仰副
陛下策士求言之盛心也臣學不足以博古才不足以通
今但所言必本於古道而不敢泛所陳必切於時事
===
而不敢畧惟
陛下不以言之淺近少加
睿覧天下幸甚愚臣幸甚干冒
天威不勝戰慄恐懼之至臣謹對

而不敢畧惟

punctuated:
之所□□者，必合乎天理；所舍者，必適□時宜。天下之大□□而益正，天下之萬目於此而益舉。由是可以格天心而正人極，由是可以貞百度而一民心，由是可以綿宗社於萬萬年之遠，而三代雍熈之盛端在今日矣。彼區區漢唐宋之治，奚足言哉！夫克臻治效之盛，一本於此心之誠如此。臣故始終以此心之誠為陛下獻者，此愚臣遇得言之時，盡獻言之誠，以仰副陛下策士求言之盛心也。
臣學不足以博古，才不足以通今，但所言必本於古道而不敢泛，所陳必切於時事而不敢畧。惟陛下不以言之淺近，少加睿覧，天下幸甚，愚臣幸甚。干冒天威，不勝戰慄恐懼之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…what is [illegible] [?] will surely accord with heavenly principle, and what is set aside will surely suit the needs of the times [?]. The great [illegible] of the realm will become still more correct [?], and its myriad affairs will thereby be carried out still more fully. Through this, you may move Heaven’s heart and rectify the highest standard for humankind; through this, you may set all institutions right and unite the people’s hearts; through this, you may perpetuate the ancestral temples and altars of state for countless ages. The flourishing harmony of the Three Dynasties will then be realized in this very day. How could the comparatively petty achievements of government under the Han, Tang, and Song merit mention! Such splendid results in government rest entirely upon the sincerity of this heart. Thus, from beginning to end, what your servant offers Your Majesty is the sincerity of this heart. Having this opportunity to speak, your ignorant servant offers his counsel with the utmost sincerity, hoping thereby to answer Your Majesty’s noble intention in examining scholars through policy questions and seeking their counsel.
Your servant’s learning is insufficient for a comprehensive knowledge of antiquity, and his ability insufficient for a thorough understanding of the present. Yet everything I say must be grounded in the Way of antiquity, and I dare not be vague; everything I present must bear directly upon current affairs, and I dare not be cursory. May Your Majesty, despite the shallowness of these words, graciously give them a little consideration. The realm would be most fortunate, and your ignorant servant most fortunate. In presuming to offend your heavenly majesty, I am overcome with trembling and the utmost fear. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
張天瑞
臣對臣聞聖王之御極也必道與法兼舉而治雍熈
之治其立法也必名與實相稱而垂遠大之圖要皆
本於一心之仁而已盖道者法之體法者道之用不
兼舉不足以言治實者名之主名者實之賓不相稱
不足以言法而仁又道法名實之本也苟心有未仁
則道法何以兼舉名實何由相稱哉古之王者所以
不患道法之不舉名實之不稱而惟患吾心之未仁
吾心既仁則以之致治必道立而法行以之立法必
名正而實稱故雍熈之治浹洽於當時遠大之圖垂
===
布於後世此夏商周三代之所以隆盛而莫或能及
之也若漢唐宋之君心在治安志存垂裕者非不欲
比迹三代之隆夫何私欲間雜仁心淪喪雖欲舉道
法而道法俱廢雖欲正名實而名實俱隳或偏陂無
輕重之倫或苟簡無本末之分其視三代之治不啻

translation_en:
Zhang Tianrui

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that when a sage king ascends the throne, he must uphold both the Way and institutional rules to bring about harmonious and flourishing government. In establishing institutions, he must ensure that names and realities correspond, thereby bequeathing a plan of far-reaching and enduring scope. In essence, all this is rooted solely in the benevolence of his heart. For the Way is the substance of institutional rules, and institutional rules are the application of the Way. Unless both are upheld, one cannot speak of good government. Reality is the master of names, and names are the guests of reality. Unless they correspond, one cannot speak of proper institutions. Benevolence, moreover, is the root of the Way, institutional rules, names, and realities. If the heart falls short of benevolence, how can the Way and institutional rules both be upheld, and how can names and realities correspond? Thus the kings of antiquity worried not that the Way and institutional rules would fail to be upheld, or that names and realities would fail to correspond, but only that their own hearts might lack benevolence. Once their hearts were benevolent, applying this to government necessarily established the Way and put institutional rules into effect; applying it to the establishment of institutions necessarily rectified names and brought realities into correspondence. Hence harmonious and flourishing government pervaded their own age, and their far-reaching plans were handed down to later generations. This is why the Three Dynasties of Xia, Shang, and Zhou flourished so greatly that none could match them.

As for those rulers of Han, Tang, and Song whose hearts were set on order and peace and whose aspirations lay in bequeathing prosperity to their descendants, it was not that they did not wish to rival the flourishing achievements of the Three Dynasties. Why, then, did selfish desires intrude and their benevolent hearts sink into ruin, so that, although they wished to uphold the Way and institutional rules, both fell into disuse, and although they wished to rectify names and realities, both collapsed? Some were biased and lacked any proper ordering of what was weighty and what was slight; others were careless and perfunctory, making no distinction between root and branch. Compared with the government of the Three Dynasties, theirs was like a stone resembling jade beside fine jade. How could they possibly rival its flourishing greatness?

We reverently reflect that Emperor Gao, Taizu of our dynasty, rose like a dragon in the Huai region and, with a benevolent heart, founded an enterprise of unsurpassed greatness. Emperor Wen[?], Taizong, pacified the dynastic house and the realm and, with a benevolent heart, [illegible verb] a foundation that would endure for ages. Renzong, Zhao… [remainder illegible]…

宣宗章皇□、英宗睿□□□，皆率由舊章，一仁心之相傳，而盡繼體守成之責。道法兼舉，名實相須，四海九州謳歌太平之盛，群黎百姓優游神化之休，聲名洋溢於八殯，治效遠追乎三代。彼區區漢唐宋之治，誠無足道矣。
欽惟皇帝陛下，以神聖之資，嗣祖宗之位，孝隆慈闈，仁被率土，天人叶應，華夏帰心。當此治平之時，似若可以少休矣，然猶體道謙冲，不自滿假，復進臣等于廷，載頒清問，用求治理。顧臣韋布之賤，何以上揆淵衷，而對揚休命乎？

translation_en:
…Xuanzong, the Zhang Emperor [?], and Yingzong, the Rui… [?], all followed the established institutions, transmitting the same benevolent heart and fully discharging their responsibility to inherit the throne and preserve its achievements. The Way and its institutions were upheld together, and names and realities sustained one another. Throughout the Four Seas and Nine Provinces, people sang of the flourishing peace; the common people enjoyed at ease the blessings of your wondrous transforming influence. Your renown spread throughout the eight distant regions [?; transcribed 八殯], and the achievements of your government matched those of the Three Dynasties of antiquity. The paltry governance of the Han, Tang, and Song truly scarcely merits mention.
I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor, endowed with divine sagacity, has succeeded to the throne of your ancestors. Your filial devotion exalts the maternal palace, and your benevolence extends throughout the realm. Heaven and humanity respond in concord, and all the Chinese lands turn their hearts toward you. At this time of orderly and peaceful rule, it might seem permissible to rest a little. Yet you continue to embody the Way in humility, without complacency. Once again you have summoned us, your servants, into the court and graciously issued your questions, seeking the means of good government. Yet how can your humble servant, a mere wearer of plain cloth, fathom your profound intentions and respond worthily to your gracious command?
Nevertheless, ordinary sayings might seem unworthy of scrutiny, yet Shun of Yu scrutinized them, for they might stir his heart toward goodness. Grass cutters and wood gatherers might seem unworthy of consultation, yet the men of old consulted them, for the highest principles might be found in their words. The Classic says: “The path to Yangyuan leads toward Muqiu.” This means that the words of the lowly may benefit the gentleman. It also says: “Like those flying birds, which are sometimes brought down by a corded arrow.” This means that even a fool’s deliberations may yield one sound insight. Foolish and lowly as I am, I have received Your Majesty’s gracious nurture and instruction, and for years have rejoiced in Your Majesty’s kindly generosity [?; characters missing]. If I do not fully set forth what I have perceived and offer the single insight that my foolishness may yield, then I shall not only fail…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
治之盛心而亦自負於平生之所抱負之所
豐臣子事
君之本心哉　竊惟昔者禹受舜禪惟精惟一而允執
厥中湯革夏正克寬克仁而顧諟明命文王則視民
如傷而止於仁武王則勝殷遏劉而建其極是皆仁
心之實而所謂精微之蘊也孟子謂三代之得天下
也以仁蓋本於此惟其有是仁心故凡道法名實皆
由是而出以言其道則君臣有義而朝廷之上肅肅
如也父子有親而家庭之間雍雍如也以言其法則
大綱小紀極綜理之周初不舉此而遺彼制度文為
===
極維持之密亦未嘗棄本而逐末其道法兼舉而無
遺如此是以當時聲教四訖式于九圍以受方國皇
以間之而成至治之休焉其立法也名正言順實與
名俱以名言之如養民之政鄉遂都鄙有貢助徹之
殊教民之政鄉黨州閭有庠序校之異以實言之則
什一為天下之中正而豪強貪暴者不容明倫為學
校之首務而梗化冥頑者無有其名實相稱而不偏
如此是以當時告厥成功受命不殆克開厥後貽厥
孫謀而享無窮之澤焉蓋嘗論夫欲善治者非道無
以立其體非法無以達諸用是不惟不相悖而實相

punctuated: 治之盛心，而亦自負於平生之所抱負之所，豐臣子事君之本心哉？竊惟昔者禹受舜禪，惟精惟一，而允執厥中；湯革夏正，克寬克仁，而顧諟明命；文王則視民如傷，而止於仁；武王則勝殷遏劉，而建其極。是皆仁心之實，而所謂精微之蘊也。孟子謂三代之得天下也以仁，蓋本於此。惟其有是仁心，故凡道法名實皆由是而出。以言其道，則君臣有義，而朝廷之上肅肅如也；父子有親，而家庭之間雍雍如也。以言其法，則大綱小紀，極綜理之周，初不舉此而遺彼；制度文為，極維持之密，亦未嘗棄本而逐末。其道法兼舉而無遺如此，是以當時聲教四訖，式于九圍，以受方國，皇以間之，而成至治之休焉。其立法也，名正言順，實與名俱。以名言之，如養民之政，鄉遂都鄙有貢助徹之殊；教民之政，鄉黨州閭有庠序校之異。以實言之，則什一為天下之中正，而豪強貪暴者不容；明倫為學校之首務，而梗化冥頑者無有。其名實相稱而不偏如此，是以當時告厥成功，受命不殆，克開厥後，貽厥孫謀，而享無窮之澤焉。蓋嘗論夫欲善治者，非道無以立其體，非法無以達諸用，是不惟不相悖，而實相
translation_en:
…Your Majesty’s earnest desire for good government, but would also betray the aspirations I have cherished throughout my life [?]. Could this accord with a subject’s fundamental intention in serving his ruler [?]?

I humbly reflect that, in antiquity, when Yu received the throne through Shun’s abdication, he remained discerning and single-minded and faithfully held to the Mean. When Tang replaced Xia’s rule, he was magnanimous and benevolent and kept Heaven’s luminous mandate constantly before him. King Wen treated the people as though they were injured and rested in benevolence. King Wu conquered Yin, put an end to slaughter, and established the supreme standard. These were all concrete expressions of a benevolent heart, constituting what is called the profound substance of subtle principles. Mencius said that the Three Dynasties gained the realm through benevolence; this was surely its foundation. Precisely because they possessed such benevolent hearts, the Way and institutions, names and realities, all issued from this source.

As for their Way, righteousness governed ruler and minister, and solemn respect prevailed at court; affection governed father and son, and harmony prevailed within households. As for their institutions, major principles and minor regulations were comprehensively ordered: they never attended to one matter while neglecting another. Their institutions, ceremonial forms, and practices were maintained with the utmost care; nor did they ever abandon the root to pursue the branches. Thus they upheld both the Way and institutions, leaving nothing unattended. Consequently, their civilizing influence reached the four quarters and provided a model throughout the nine regions; they received the allegiance of the regional states and greatly intervened among them [?], achieving the splendor of perfect government.

In establishing institutions, their names were correct and their pronouncements accorded with them; realities accompanied names. In terms of names, policies for sustaining the people distinguished among the gong, zhu, and che systems of taxation in the xiang and sui districts, domains, and outlying settlements. Policies for educating the people distinguished among the xiang, xu, and xiao schools in the xiang, dang, zhou, and lü local units. In terms of realities, a levy of one-tenth was the just standard for the realm, leaving no room for powerful bullies or the greedy and violent; clarifying human relationships was the foremost task of schools, and none remained obstinately resistant to moral transformation. Thus names and realities corresponded without imbalance. Consequently, they could announce the completion of their achievements, receive the mandate without peril, open the way for their successors, and bequeath plans to their descendants, who enjoyed their inexhaustible blessings.

I have reflected that those who desire good government cannot establish its essential substance without the Way, nor give effect to its practical functions without institutions. These therefore not only do not contradict one another, but indeed mutually…

title: 成化十七年進士登科錄
text:
求也彼羅仲素謂三代之治在道而不在法者雖
講原之論然質以孟子聖人既竭心思繼之
以不忍人之政之說則所繼者政而所以繼之者道
也是道亦寓於法而法非無所用矣夫何戾邪次立
法者非名無以表實非實無以正名是不惟不相戾
而又必相須也彼羅仲素謂三代之法貴實而不貴
名者雖曰崇質務實之評然考諸衛君待孔子為政
而孔子有必也正名之說則所正者名而所以正之
者實也是名必根於實而正名在所先矣夫何迂邪
若夫繼周而王者漢也漢有天下如高祖發義帝之
喪戮丁公之叛則君臣之義以明納四皓之請定儲
貳之建則父子之親以篤其於綱常倫紀為不失故
說者謂漢之大綱正焉然大綱雖正而有所未純况賈
誼請興禮樂而文帝讓以未遑仲舒請興學校而武
帝梏於私欲取士雖有四科之目而譽髦斯士之遺
意不存約法雖有三章之格而刑期無刑之典則無
有是萬目之有所未舉也此漢之治所以終於雜霸
而無以入周焉文中子論漢取高文武宣光武明
章為七制就七制之中而論其知重道者則明帝之
重儒臨雍拜老似為獨優然亦過於察慧世不

求也。彼羅仲素謂三代之治在道而不在法者，雖講原之論，然質以孟子「聖人既竭心思，繼之以不忍人之政」之說，則所繼者政，而所以繼之者道也。是道亦寓於法，而法非無所用矣，夫何戾邪？次立法者，非名無以表實，非實無以正名，是不惟不相戾，而又必相須也。彼羅仲素謂三代之法貴實而不貴名者，雖曰崇質務實之評，然考諸衛君待孔子為政，而孔子有「必也正名」之說，則所正者名，而所以正之者實也。是名必根於實，而正名在所先矣，夫何迂邪？
若夫繼周而王者，漢也。漢有天下，如高祖發義帝之喪，戮丁公之叛，則君臣之義以明；納四皓之請，定儲貳之建，則父子之親以篤。其於綱常倫紀為不失，故說者謂漢之大綱正焉。然大綱雖正，而有所未純。况賈誼請興禮樂，而文帝讓以未遑；仲舒請興學校，而武帝梏於私欲。取士雖有四科之目，而譽髦斯士之遺意不存；約法雖有三章之格，而刑期無刑之典則無有。是萬目之有所未舉也。此漢之治所以終於雜霸，而無以入周焉。文中子論漢，取高、文、武、宣、光武、明、章為七制。就七制之中而論其知重道者，則明帝之重儒，臨雍拜老，似為獨優。然亦過於察慧，世不

…require one another. Luo Zhongsu’s assertion that the government of the Three Dynasties rested on the Way rather than on laws may be an argument examining first principles [?]. Yet, tested against Mencius’s statement, “The sages, having exhausted their minds and thoughts, followed this with government that could not bear the suffering of others,” what followed was government, while that by which they carried it forward was the Way. Thus the Way also resides in laws, and laws are by no means without a function. How, then, could they conflict? Next, those who establish laws cannot express substance without names, nor rectify names without substance. These not only do not conflict; they necessarily depend upon one another. Luo Zhongsu’s assertion that the laws of the Three Dynasties valued substance rather than names may be described as a judgment honoring substance and practical realities. Yet consider how, when the ruler of Wei awaited Confucius’s assistance in governing, Confucius declared, “It must be the rectification of names.” What was to be rectified was names, while the means of rectifying them was substance. Thus names must be rooted in substance, and rectifying names must come first. How, then, could this be impractical?
As for the dynasty that succeeded Zhou in ruling the realm, it was Han. When Han possessed the empire, Gaozu proclaimed mourning for Emperor Yi and executed Ding Gong for his treachery, thereby making clear the righteousness binding ruler and minister. He accepted the plea of the Four Hoary Elders and settled the establishment of the heir apparent, thereby strengthening the affection between father and son. In its fundamental bonds, constant virtues, and ordered human relationships, Han did not fail; hence commentators say that Han’s principal framework was correct. Yet although that framework was correct, it was not entirely pure. Moreover, Jia Yi requested the promotion of rites and music, but Emperor Wen declined on the grounds that he had not yet had the leisure to attend to them. Zhongshu requested the establishment of schools, but Emperor Wu was constrained by selfish desires. Although the selection of officials had its four categories, the inherited intent of praising and encouraging worthy scholars had not survived. Although the simplification of the laws had its framework of three articles, there were no established principles embodying the aim of using punishments to bring about a condition in which punishments were unnecessary. Thus many particulars remained unimplemented. This is why Han government ultimately remained mixed with the methods of hegemons and could not attain the standard of Zhou. In discussing Han, Wenzhongzi selected the reigns of Gaozu, Wen, Wu, Xuan, Guangwu, Ming, and Zhang as the seven exemplary regimes. Among these seven, if we consider who understood the importance of honoring the Way, Emperor Ming seems to have been especially outstanding in his respect for Confucian scholars, his visits to the Imperial University, and his ceremonial homage to elders. Yet he too was excessively given to searching scrutiny and cleverness; the age did not [?]…

府之分制刑有三覆奏五覆奏除斷趾禁笞背之例

繼漢而王者，唐也。唐有天下，如高祖立法：丁中之民給田一頃，篤疾減什之六，寡妻妾減什之七，皆以什之二為世業，而田賦之制以行。太宗之制兵，八百人為下府，千人為中府，萬人為上府之分；制刑，有三覆奏、五覆奏，除斷趾、禁笞背之例，而兵刑之法以定。其於制度條目頗詳悉，故說者謂唐之萬目舉焉。然萬目雖舉，而有所未盡。况太宗之脅父臣虜，而虧君臣父子之道；戕亂閨門，而無兄弟夫婦之倫；高宗之貽禍家邦，明皇之腥穢人紀，是大綱又有所未正也。此唐之治所以竟為雜夷，而不相遠於漢焉。歐陽子論唐，取太宗、玄宗、憲宗為三宗。就三宗之中而論其能守法者，則憲宗之剛明果斷，能用忠謀，似為獨賢；然亦晚年信奸溺邪，世不能無議焉。漢唐之所以一止於雜霸、一止於雜夷如此者，庸非仁心之未盡，而道法不能兼舉，名實不能相稱歟？
至若繼唐而有天下者，宋也。議者謂其大綱則正，萬目未盡舉，又若有所劣於唐矣。然考之當時，宰執吕大防進言，以為：「祖宗以來，事母后皆朝夕見。仁宗以姪事姑，□人禮宮禁之極，内外之嚴，貴戚得駕馭之術，恭儉之尚，儉勤身之矩矱，皆祖宗家法所以致太平者。」
translation_en:
The dynasty that succeeded the Han in ruling the realm was the Tang. When the Tang possessed all under Heaven, Gaozu, for example, established laws granting one qing of land to males in the adult and intermediate age categories. The allotment was reduced by six-tenths for the severely disabled and by seven-tenths for widowed wives and concubines; in each case, two-tenths constituted a hereditary holding. Thus the system of land allotment and taxation was put into effect. Taizong organized the military into lower garrisons of eight hundred men, middle garrisons of one thousand, and upper garrisons of ten thousand [?]. In regulating punishments, he established provisions for three or five repeated submissions to the throne for review, abolished the cutting off of toes, and prohibited flogging on the back. Thus military and penal regulations were established. His institutional arrangements were quite detailed, and commentators therefore say that under the Tang the myriad particulars of government were put into effect. Yet, although these particulars were implemented, some remained incomplete. Moreover, Taizong coerced his father into submitting as a subject to the barbarians, compromising the Way governing ruler and subject, father and son. Through killing and disorder within his household, he violated the proper relations between brothers and between husband and wife. Gaozong bequeathed calamity to his house and realm, while Minghuang defiled the fundamental human relationships. Thus the guiding principles, too, were not wholly correct. This is why Tang government ultimately remained adulterated with barbarian practices and differed little from that of the Han. In discussing the Tang, Master Ouyang singled out Taizong, Xuanzong, and Xianzong as its three exemplary sovereigns. Among these three, if we consider their ability to uphold the laws, Xianzong seems outstandingly worthy: firm, discerning, and decisive, he could employ loyal counsel. Yet in his later years he too trusted the treacherous and became immersed in pernicious practices, so later generations could not refrain from criticism. That the Han and Tang stopped respectively at government adulterated with hegemonic practices and government adulterated with barbarian practices—was this not because their benevolent intentions were incompletely realized, so that the Way and its institutional rules could not both be implemented, and name and reality could not accord?
As for the dynasty that succeeded the Tang in possessing all under Heaven, it was the Song. Critics say that its guiding principles were correct but that its myriad particulars were not fully implemented; in this respect it would seem somewhat inferior to the Tang. Yet examination of that period shows that Chief Councilor Lü Dafang submitted this argument: “From the founding ancestors onward, the emperors attended upon the empress dowagers morning and evening. Renzong served his aunt as a nephew should. [An illegible character and an unclear passage concerning human propriety and the palace precincts follow here.] The strict separation of inner and outer quarters, the methods for keeping imperial relatives under control, the esteem for reverence and frugality, and the standards of personal frugality and diligence [?]—these were all ancestral house rules by which great peace was achieved…”

…the worthiness of □□ [?]. Thus, when the court historians called Taizu an outstanding and benevolent ruler, they spoke of his intelligence, benevolence [illegible], broad understanding, and magnanimity. When they said that Taizong possessed the strategic capacity of an emperor, they judged him by his benevolence, forbearance, reverence, and frugality, his love of learning, and his preservation of the inherited achievement. Zhenzong was generous, benevolent, compassionate, and loving; to say that he possessed the magnanimity of an emperor was certainly no excessive praise. Renzong was reverent, frugal, benevolent, and forbearing; to call him a ruler of utmost benevolence was likewise no exaggerated posthumous tribute. These four sage rulers succeeded one another, bringing a century of peace: this may indeed be called flourishing. In what respect was it inferior to the Han and Tang? Yet their benevolent hearts were not entirely pure [illegible], the Way and its institutions were never fully put into practice, and names and realities sometimes failed to correspond. Thus the Song remained merely the Song and ultimately could not rival the flourishing grandeur of the Three Dynasties.

Institutions do not operate on their own: they must originate in the Way. Names must not be established arbitrarily: they must be rooted in realities. To put the Way and its institutions into practice and rectify names and realities, grounding all of these in the heart’s benevolence—this is why the Three Dynasties flourished so greatly, while even the outstanding and righteous rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song could not approach a ten-thousandth part of their achievement.

Now Your Majesty has addressed a policy question to your servant, expressing the wish to explore the subtle depths of the Way and investigate in detail the establishment of institutions. As for what are called names and realities, you likewise wish to investigate why, under the Three Dynasties, they depended upon one another and brought good government, whereas under the Han, Tang, and Song they did not depend upon one another, and government fell short of antiquity. You hope thereby to distinguish clearly what should be adopted and what rejected, so that bringing the world to harmony and prosperity may become an attainable prospect. Foolish though your servant is, I recognize from this that Your Majesty’s heart is a heart that extends benevolence to all under Heaven. Moreover, the common people throughout the realm [?] now wholeheartedly turn toward perfect government, and Your Majesty applies yourself resolutely to this as well. How, then, could the practice of government fail to attain harmony and prosperity?

The Way originates in the heart; institutions manifest themselves in affairs. Since the Way of the Three Kings originated in their hearts, if Your Majesty wishes to [illegible] its subtle depths, you should seek these in the principles governing the Three Kings’ hearts, such as refinement, singleness of purpose, and holding fast to [illegible; remainder doubtful]. The institutions of the Three Kings manifested themselves in affairs …

…the details of institutions and regulations [?] should be examined in the accomplishments of the Three Kings, such as the well-field system and schools [?]. Substance serves to rectify names, and names serve to express substance. Under the Three Dynasties, names and substance sustained one another, and … [?]. I hope Your Majesty will adopt this and put it into practice. Under the Han, Tang, and Song, names and substance did not sustain one another, and government fell short of antiquity. Your servant hopes Your Majesty will reject this and refrain from such conduct. Yet what enables one to adopt the former and put it into practice, and to reject the latter and refrain from it, is nothing other than making one’s heart benevolent.
Your servant was born and raised in humble circumstances. I have heard that Your Majesty implements the Way and its institutions with a benevolent heart. To attain this briefly and then abruptly lose it is unacceptable; one must remain consistent over both long and short periods. I have heard that Your Majesty rectifies names and substance with a benevolent heart. To be diligent at the outset but negligent at the end is unacceptable; one must remain the same from beginning to end.
Whether in private life, in conducting affairs, or in dealing with others, there are times of activity and times of stillness. To fail to preserve the heart is no way to practice benevolence. One must preserve the heart in these circumstances, without allowing activity or stillness to alter it. Whether concerning the court, the officials, or the myriad people, there are distinctions of distance, near and far. To allow this heart even a brief lapse is no way to perfect benevolence. One must preserve the heart in these matters, without letting distance occasion any neglect. If seeing and hearing do not accord with ritual propriety, the benevolent heart will thereby be injured and diminished. One must adhere wholly to ritual propriety and make one’s safeguards as thorough as possible. If speech and action do not accord with ritual propriety, the benevolent heart will thereby be obscured and eroded. One must adhere wholly to ritual propriety and maintain the firmest resolve. Promote exemplary men and dismiss petty men, thereby nurturing this heart and strengthening one’s benevolence. Repudiate heterodox teachings and honor orthodox learning, thereby rectifying this heart and perfecting one’s benevolence. punctuated: □□吾之仁心，而不使之痿痺。若然，則人欲日消，□日明，道法由是而可舉，名實由是而可正，□□之業可綿亘於無窮，三代之治又豈不可追復於今日哉？先儒胡仁仲有云：「仁心，立政之本。」要之，舉道法而正名實，祖述禹湯文武之道，憲章祖宗列聖之法，以洽雍熙□□，以垂遠大之圖，一皆本於此。臣敢以是為終篇獻。伏願陛下萬幾之暇，少垂睿覽而留意焉，則宗社幸甚，天下幸甚，萬世幸甚！□天威，不勝戰慄恐懼之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: …[?] my humane heart, and keep it from becoming numb and unresponsive. If this is so, selfish desires will diminish daily, and [?] will grow brighter daily. The teachings and institutions of the Way can thereby be put into practice, and names and realities brought into proper accord. The undertaking of [?] can endure forever; how, then, could the good government of the Three Dynasties not be restored today? The earlier Confucian scholar Hu Renzhong said: “A humane heart is the foundation of government.” In sum, putting the teachings and institutions of the Way into practice and rectifying names and realities, carrying forward the Way of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, taking as models the institutions of your ancestral sovereigns, bringing about harmony and prosperity [?], and handing down a plan of far-reaching and enduring scope—all are rooted in this. Your servant ventures to offer this as the conclusion of his essay. I humbly hope that Your Majesty, in a moment of leisure amid the myriad affairs of state, will graciously read it and give it consideration. Then how fortunate would be the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain, how fortunate all under Heaven, and how fortunate the countless generations to come! [?] Your Majesty’s awe-inspiring presence, I cannot restrain my trembling and utmost fear. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.
